name: Front parlor (period furniture, rugs, drapes)
note: Dampened above 1 kHz, woody lows, very short decay; close-mic intimacy.

name: Carpeted bedroom
note: Short reflections eaten by carpet and soft furniture; midrange-forward; very close, no tail.

name: Hardwood-floor living room
note: Some early reflections off floor and walls; modest tail; midrange honk if low ceiling.

name: Kitchen (tile floor, hard counters)
note: Hard reflections, comb-filtering on voice, bright presence-band, short flutter.

name: Tile bathroom
note: Dense early reflections, bright, short-but-dense decay, the shower-vocal sound.

name: Closet (vocal booth makeshift)
note: Short, dry, slight box-resonance, very close. The post-2010 DIY makeshift vocal-booth — a closet with clothes-as-absorber lining. Common in bedroom-pop and TikTok-era streaming-pop tracking.

name: Stairwell (concrete-and-steel)
note: Strong vertical mode, long thin tail, drum-room for huge percussive tail.

name: Hallway
note: Strong axial mode, slap delays, narrow image. Long parallel walls create a single-axis flutter and pinched-midrange tubular character. Useful for narrative-spoken-word and lo-fi production deliberately seeking the hallway character.

name: Treated recording studio (dead booth)
note: Decay essentially zero, no early reflections, full presence and zero ambience — the in-your-face sound.

name: Treated live room (reflective but controlled)
note: Engineered early reflections, decay around half a second, frequency-balanced — the good drum room.

name: Untreated bedroom studio
note: Standing waves below 200 Hz, flutter echoes between parallel walls, the DIY sound.

name: Speakeasy / jazz club (low-ceilinged)
note: Furniture and bodies dampen reflections, midrange-forward, short tail — everyone is close.

name: Honky-tonk / dance hall (long rectangular wood-paneled)
note: Length means strong axial slap, wood paneling adds midrange resonance; you hear distance from stage.

name: Pentecostal storefront church
note: Short bright tail, drop-ceiling absorbs highs unevenly, lots of early reflections.

name: AM radio booth / broadcast booth
note: Treated for proximity-effect-on-purpose, narrow band, lo-fi historical character.

name: Irish pub (interior, low ceiling, full of drinkers)
note: Bodies absorb most reflections, wood adds warmth, glass clatter and conversation as bed.

name: Cathedral (stone gothic)
note: Decay 4–10+ seconds, dense diffusion, low-frequency boom piles up; only slow music survives.

name: Stone parish church
note: Decay around 2–4 seconds, balanced spectrum, classical canonical.

name: Wooden country church
note: Wood absorbs highs, modest tail (~1–1.5s), congregation-warm.

name: Wooden barn (large, hayloft)
note: Soft reflective wood, hay absorbs unpredictably, drafts add air; country-roomy sound.

name: Tin-roofed shack
note: Metal roof reflects highs hard, wooden walls give midrange — gospel and blues vernacular.

name: Concrete basement
note: Hard floor, low ceiling, parallel walls — strong room modes, the garage-band thump.

name: Treated concert hall (shoebox)
note: Decay 1.8–2.2 seconds, even diffusion, classical canonical.

name: Gymnasium (high school)
note: Polished wood floor, painted block walls, parallel surfaces — school-dance canonical.

name: Subway tunnel
note: Strong axial mode, low-frequency build-up, voices arrive as if from far away with comb-filtered slap.

name: Adobe room
note: Thick walls absorb deep, short tail, dry top end, southwestern canonical.

name: Tape echo chamber (purpose-built reflective room)
note: Engineered decay, lush mid-band, mid-twentieth-century recording canonical.

name: Open prairie / open field
note: No reflections, sound dies in air absorption, voice sits naked; vast-and-empty character.

name: Bayou porch (rocking chair on)
note: Wood porch boards reflect a little, vegetation absorbs the rest, insect bed fills tail.

name: Beach (oceanfront)
note: No hard reflections, surf as constant low-end pink noise, lonely-and-wide.

name: Forest clearing
note: Trees scatter reflections diffusely, very short tail, leaves and birds in bed.

name: Mountain valley
note: Single specular slap from opposite face, gap of seconds, then bright return — epic-and-cold.

name: Outdoor festival stage (PA reinforced)
note: Direct from stage plus delay-tower reinforcement, wind affecting top, crowd as broadband bed.

name: Field recording (handheld, ambient)
note: Whatever the actual space is, plus handling noise, breath, capsule self-noise.

name: Truck cab (interior, driving)
note: Glass and metal panels reflect, dashboard absorbs irregularly, road noise as low-mid bed.

name: Phone line / call (codec'd)
note: 300–3400 Hz, codec artifacts, codec swirl on consonants.

name: Walkie-talkie / shortwave
note: Heavy compression, AM-style distortion, intermittent.

name: Cassette tape (medium, doubling as space)
note: Bias noise, wow-and-flutter, top end rolled — heard as the space the sound exists inside.

name: Inside a piano (sustain pedal down)
note: Strings vibrate in sympathy with anything in the room — ghostly chordal bed.

name: Canyon / amphitheatre rock-walls
note: Discrete delays from canyon walls, no diffuse reverb (no enclosing roof). Singular slap-echo where Western soundtracks and outdoor ceremony ritual happen.

name: Urban courtyard (between buildings)
note: Outdoor but enclosed on multiple sides by hard urban walls. Short slap-back vertically, traffic and city ambient as low-mid bed. The "alleyway recording" envelope — cypher rap, busker session, found-sound.

name: Ice cave / glacier surface
note: Hard ice walls reflect the high frequencies most outdoor environments absorb. Tail decay can rival cathedral spaces while staying brighter and harder. Rare in commercial recording, definitive when used.

name: Marsh / wetland lowland
note: Water surface absorbs lows; humidity attenuates highs; biological sound bed (frogs, insects, water) is dense. Rural blues, Cajun-bayou recording, naturalist field-recording.

name: Wireless earbud / Bluetooth codec
note: SBC/AAC/aptX/LC3 codec compression as the listening envelope. Cymbal smear, transient softening, dynamic-range collapse. The actual listening medium for most modern streaming.

name: Boombox / portable speaker
note: Small full-range driver in plastic housing, bass via port resonance, distortion at usable listening volumes. The block-party / cookout / beach-day playback chain — boom-bap and reggaeton are mixed for it.

name: Electrical-era converted-office studio (1925–45)
note: Converted Manhattan office spaces with hung blankets and a single ribbon-isolated cutting lathe. Roughly 15-30 m² with bare walls behind absorbent fabric. The transition space from acoustic-horn to electrical-mic recording — where the 1925-1932 American commercial recordings were made.

name: Swing-era large live tracking room (1935–55)
note: Large live tracking room (~250 m²), proscenium-like layout, high ceiling, hardwood floor, hard rear wall. Multi-mic capability mixed to single mono master. Defining workflow: full ensemble tracked simultaneously with strategic mic placement substituting for multitrack isolation.

name: Early-tape American small commercial (1948–65)
note: Small American commercial room (~50 m²), partially treated, characteristic dry-but-alive acoustic. Chess Studios at Cottage Grove, Sun Studio at 706 Union, J&M Studio in New Orleans defined this scale-tier. Small enough that the room sound bonded the rhythm section together; treated enough that vocals could overdub cleanly.

name: Small-LA studio with reverb chambers (1958–70)
note: Small tracking room (~30 m²) coupled to two purpose-built reverb chambers as primary sound-shaping element. Gold Star's tile-walled chambers, Western Recorders' chamber stack. The tracking-room-plus-chambers compound is the architectural unit; neither alone produces the sound.

name: Multitrack flagship American studio (1985–2000)
note: Late-analog major-rock infrastructure: Sound City Studio A late-80s/90s, Bear Creek (Woodinville WA), Pachyderm (Cannon Falls MN), Bearsville NY, A&M Studios (LA late-80s/90s). SSL E and G-series consoles paired with classic British-style tracking outboard. Studer A800 tape with Pro Tools first-generation adoption late in the era. EMT plates remained standard, AMS/Eventide digital delays became ubiquitous.

name: British class-A commercial studio (1965–85)
note: Often converted Victorian church halls, theatres, or large drawing-rooms. Wessex (former church hall in Highbury), Olympic (former cinema in Barnes), Trident (former cinema in Soho), AIR (top of Oxford Circus). Large naturally-reverberant English commercial-rooms paired with iron-transformer console signal flow.

name: Small London commercial studio (1962–1968)
note: De Lane Lea (Soho), IBC, Pye Studios Marble Arch, Regent Sound. Small London commercial rooms (~30–40 m²), tube-console era, 4-track quarter-inch tape standard. Distinct from the later large 1965-85 class-A British rooms by both scale (small) and era (predates 8-track multitrack adoption). Defining feature: producer-led tight tracking workflow under aggressive time pressure — single-take takes were common. The architectural sibling of Chess Studios and Sun Studio in scale, but with British engineering and tracking conventions.

name: LA mid-major rock commercial (1970–95)
note: Sound City (Van Nuys), A&M Studios (Hollywood, a converted silent-film lot), Cherokee, Conway. Large tracking-room paired with Neve-school console. Sound City's Studio A live room with the Neve 8028 produced drum sounds across thirty years of mid-major LA rock-tracking sessions.

name: EMI Lagos / African commercial (1965–85)
note: EMI Lagos (Apapa), Decca West Africa, Phonogram Lagos. Large tropical-climate commercial studio (~150 m²) sized for full Africa-70-style ensemble tracking. EMI/Marconi tube console heritage, Studer A80 tape, BBC limiter influence — European-equipment-mix for African popular-music recording.

name: Late-70s NYC commercial (1975–85)
note: Sigma Sound NYC, Sweet Mountain Recorders NJ, Sound Ideas, Calliope Studios. Small-medium commercial rooms with early-digital-reverb adoption (EMT 250 deployed at top studios from 1976). The transitional environment between analog-only flagship and digital-multitrack-era.

name: American indie-commercial mid-80s (1980–2000)
note: Total Access (Redondo Beach), Inner Ear (Arlington VA), Easley-McCain (Memphis), small-room engineer-owned tracking spaces. Commercial studios specifically positioned for underground bands — economically constrained, not aesthetically choosing vintage. A genuine third commercial scale-tier.

name: Pacific Northwest commercial-rock (1985–2005)
note: Bear Creek (Woodinville), Avast! (Seattle), Studio Litho (Seattle), Pachyderm (Cannon Falls MN). Regional mid-major American commercial-rock studios that proliferated during the alt-rock major-label boom. Distinct from LA flagship rooms by both region and budget-tier.

name: Vintage-revival small-analog studio (1995–pres)
note: Toe Rag Studios London (no equipment newer than 1963 ostensibly), Sun Studio reactivated, the earliest Easley-McCain. Vintage-revival is its own scale-tier — the room and chain ARE the production aesthetic. Distinct from indie-commercial (which is economically constrained) by being aesthetically deliberate.

name: Remote-isolation cabin / rural DIY (2005–pres)
note: Wisconsin hunting cabin, rural farmhouse home recordings, isolated rural sessions. Remote domestic-living recording space — not bedroom, not auteur-professional-home, not pre-DAW pioneer. The deliberate-isolation analog-acoustic DIY archetype that proliferated in 2007-onward indie-folk.

name: Atlanta trap-production commercial (2010–pres)
note: Patchwerk, Stankonia, Doppler, and other Atlanta commercial rooms. Vocal booth + producer workstation + lounge-as-creative-space. Beat-already-existing-when-vocal-tracked workflow. Defined the trap-era recording aesthetic — autotune-as-composition, dramatic vocal compression, modern digital chain throughout.

name: K-pop idol-pop production complex (2010–pres)
note: HYBE complex (formerly Big Hit), SM Entertainment, JYP Entertainment, YG Entertainment. Multi-room facilities with vocal-tracking-isolated booth + MIDI production room + mixing room as discrete workflow stages. Sessions cross-collaborated with Korean A&R, Swedish/American songwriters, Korean mixing engineers in sequence.

name: Auteur professional-grade home studio
note: Self-built compound studios, mountain residences with attached recording facilities, English country-house studios, urban industrial-loft conversions. Professional-grade gear in a domestic space — distinct from bedroom (DAW-era hobbyist) and from electronic-pioneer-home (technology-pioneer). The defining workflow: solo-multitrack auteur production with full creative control.

name: Cross-continental distributed production (2015–pres)
note: No single physical tracking room. Vocals tracked at one studio, beat made in another, mixing in a third. Pro Tools session passed across countries via cloud collaboration. Globalized 2020s pop production workflow — the recording is composed across multiple discrete tracking environments without a unified room sound.

name: Saharan broadcast-station booth (Kidal/Tamanrasset)
note: Single-story cement-block radio station with carpet and minimal foam treatment. Solar-power-only operation forces nocturnal tracking. Radio Tisdas (Kidal, Mali) is the archetype: small, dry, no live chamber, ambience added at mix. Tuareg desert blues canon traces here.

name: Saharan stone-walled village courtyard
note: Stone-walled village courtyards in Tessalit, Imidiwan, and surrounding settlements. Mobile-rig tracking with ambient capture; natural wind suppression by stone walls. Used for the post-Radio-Tisdas Tuareg canon when permanent studios are inaccessible.

name: Outdoor Saharan plateau (anechoic-leaning)
note: Tassili n'Ajjer plateau, Joshua Tree, open-desert outdoor sessions. No walls, no reflections, near-anechoic capture with desert wind bedded under. Tuareg canon late-career outdoor sessions trace here.

name: North-African medina stone-and-plaster room
note: Marrakesh and Essaouira medina rooms — stone floors, plaster walls, courtyard reverberation. Naturally live, not added in mix. The Axiom-label Gnawa canon (Marrakesh medina 1990) traces here. Distinct from Western studio rooms by hard-surface live-acoustic signature.

name: Intimate Paris small-studio (Lusafrica 1988–2011)
note: Studio Bastille, Studio de la Madeleine, Studio Music dAnge and kindred small-to-medium Paris rooms with wood floors and soft treatment. None standard alone; the morna acoustic is the cluster. Vocals dry-to-medium; violin and clarinet sit in modest plate decay. The Lusafrica morna canon traces here.

name: Addis Ababa radio/private studio (1969–74)
note: Empire-era radio facility and private studio rooms in Addis Ababa where the Amha/Kaifa/Philips Ethiopia catalog was tracked. Live-band one-take sessions. Lacquers cut and pressed in India, Lebanon, Greece, and shipped back. Ethio-jazz Golden Age (1969–74) traces here. Distinct from any Western 1970s studio room.

name: Port of Spain community studio (1979–pres)
note: Sea-Sand Studios, KH Studios, Semp Studios — Port of Spain studios that supported rapso, soca, and calypso production from the late 1970s onward. Mid-tier British console class; dry mix-aesthetic. The Port of Spain rapso canon traces here. Distinct from the Brooklyn Caribbean-diaspora label and studio context.

name: Brent Black Music Co-Op (London 1980s)
note: Brent Black Music Co-Op (Harlesden, NW London), the Caribbean-UK diaspora community studio. Brother Resistances 1986 Rapso Take Over album was tracked here. Community-grade Soundcraft/MCI-class console, Shure dynamics throughout, no live chamber. Dub-influenced mix aesthetic with tape echo on vocals.

name: Phonogram / Philips Brasil studio (Rio + SP, 1965–1985)
note: Philips Brasil studios (later Phonogram, then PolyGram) in Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo were the dominant major-label tracking context for MPB and the Tropicália aftermath from the mid-1960s onward. Mid-tier European consoles (Neumann, Telefunken, EMI-derived), 8 then 16-track analog tape. The core MPB singer-songwriter canon traces here. The Tropicália orchestral-arrangement school dominates the 1968–1972 aesthetic. Distinct from the smaller Estúdios Scatena and Estúdio Eldorado.

name: Estúdios Scatena (São Paulo, 1967–1970s)
note: Estúdios Scatena in São Paulo, where a canonical Tropicália debut was tracked December 1967–January 1968. Small-room live tracking, 4-track then 8-track tape, characteristic tape-effect and musique-concrète collage aesthetic of the Tropicália canon. Distinct from Phonogram Brasil major-label rooms.

name: Mocambo / Rozenblit Recife studio (1954–mid-1980s)
note: The Mocambo / Rozenblit record factory, founded 11 June 1954 in the Afogados district of Recife, with the Mocambo label as its main sub-label for Northeast Brazilian regional music. By the mid-1960s the operation held roughly 22% of the Brazilian phonographic market. Mocambo-label sessions for the frevo canon, plus baião, maracatu, samba-canção, and bolero. Repeated Capibaribe-river floods (1966, 1967, 1970, 1975, 1977) damaged the plant. Closed mid-1980s.

name: Bahian terreiro (Salvador, candomblé ritual)
note: Bahian candomblé terreiros — semi-outdoor ritual courtyards with roof but open walls, stone or packed-earth floors, surrounding kitchen and dressing rooms. Atabaque trio (rum/rumpi/lê) tracked acoustically with natural courtyard decay. Anthropological field recordings preserve this acoustic; commercial liturgical recordings rare and usually mono-portable. Distinct from any indoor studio.

name: Escola de samba quadra (Rio, outdoor rehearsal)
note: Escola de samba quadras — outdoor or large-roofed rehearsal spaces in Rio favelas and Zona Norte where samba schools rehearse the bateria for Carnival. Massive percussion section (200+ surdos, repiniques, tamborins, chocalhos, cuícas, agogôs) tracked with multi-mic capture. Distinct from intimate samba-canção parlor recording.

name: Roda de capoeira (outdoor circle)
note: Roda de capoeira — the small outdoor circle (5-8m diameter) where capoeira is played. Three berimbaus (gunga, médio, viola) plus atabaque, two pandeiros, agogô, reco-reco, and circle of clappers/singers. Beach or packed-earth surface. Distinct from any indoor performance space; codex must not default to open prairie.

name: Rio favela home-production (baile funk)
note: Rio favela home-production setups for baile funk — bedroom DAWs (Acid Pro, FL Studio, Fruity Loops, then Logic and Ableton), consumer monitors, USB-interface bedroom rigs. The Tamborzão beat is the foundational pattern. Furacão 2000 sound-system distribution context. Distinct from professional Rio studios; this is the actual favela home-rig acoustic.

name: Javanese pendopo (traditional gamelan pavilion)
note: Javanese pendopo — the open-walled pavilion (typically wooden columns, joglo or limasan roof, marble or terracotta floor) where Javanese gamelan is performed in kraton courts (Yogyakarta, Surakarta) and at wayang kulit performances. The pavilion architecture creates substantial natural reverberation, sympathetic bronze resonance across the 20-30 instrument ensemble, and outdoor coupling. Distinct from any indoor studio; field recordings and the Smithsonian Folkways gamelan canon trace here.

name: Balinese banjar / pura courtyard
note: Balinese banjar (community pavilion) and pura (temple) courtyards where the gong kebyar, gender wayang, and other Balinese gamelan ensembles perform during odalan temple festivals. Tropical outdoor acoustics, paired male/female bronze instruments tuned slightly apart for the characteristic shimmering beats. Distinct from Javanese pendopo by tighter, faster, brighter ensemble.

name: Tatami parlor (Japanese chamber / honkyoku)
note: Japanese tatami-floored chamber room — paper shoji walls, wood ceiling, woven straw mat floor. Highly damped acoustic, intimate close-listening environment for shakuhachi honkyoku, koto-shakuhachi-shamisen sankyoku chamber music, and other intimate traditional contexts. The opposite of a reverberant gamelan pendopo: very dry, very close. Distinct from the larger noh and kabuki performance spaces.

name: Noh stage (Japanese ritual theater)
note: Noh stage — characteristic cypress-wood floor with sand pit beneath (for sympathetic resonance), pillared roof over the stage even when indoors, painted matsu pine on the kagami-ita rear panel. The shomendokoro audience seats face the stage at distance. Hayashi musicians (nōkan flute, ko-tsuzumi shoulder drum, ō-tsuzumi hip drum, taiko stick drum) sit upstage. Vocal style is sustained, declamatory. Distinct from kabuki theater.

name: Kabuki theater (Edo-Tokyo classical)
note: Kabuki theater — large wooden auditorium with hanamichi runway extending into audience. Kabuki-bayashi musicians (geza ensemble) play offstage; nagauta shamisen-and-voice ensembles play onstage. Wood-floor projection, audience-distance vocal style. Distinct from noh by larger scale, more elaborate sets, and pop-stylized vocal delivery.

name: Mongolian ger (yurt) interior
note: Mongolian ger (yurt) interior — circular felt-wall tent, ~5m diameter, wood lattice frame, central stove. Highly damped acoustic from felt walls; intimate domestic context for urtyn duu (long-song), morin khuur solo, and khoomei overtone singing in community-circle settings. Smithsonian Folkways, King Records (Japan) Mongolian field recordings trace here. Distinct from the outdoor steppe context.

name: Mongolian steppe outdoor
note: Mongolian outdoor steppe — near-anechoic vast plain, used for ceremonial urtyn duu (long-song), morin khuur, and overtone singing in herding contexts. Wind suppression critical for field recording. The vocal projection necessary for outdoor performance shapes the form itself — long sustained tones, ornamented melismas. Distinct from indoor ger acoustic.

name: Tibetan monastery assembly hall (du-khang)
note: Tibetan monastery du-khang assembly hall — stone walls, painted wood columns, often 8-15m ceiling, hundreds of seated monks. Long natural reverberation supports multiphonic chant (Gyuto, Gyume tantric colleges) and the ritual brass-and-percussion ensemble (dungchen, gyaling, kangling thigh-trumpets, rolmo cymbals, nga drums). Field recordings on Folkways and Real World trace here.

name: Chinese traditional teahouse (chaguan)
note: Chinese traditional teahouse — wooden architecture, small intimate halls (Shanghai, Suzhou, Hangzhou, Chengdu styles), bamboo-and-wood furnishings, intimate listening with tea service. Context for guqin solo, wenrenyue literati chamber music, pingtan storytelling-and-song (Suzhou). Distinct from the modern Chinese conservatory recording context.

name: Shanghai EMI Pathé / Great China studio (1930s-40s)
note: Pre-revolutionary Shanghai EMI Pathé and Great China studios in the French Concession — the recording infrastructure for Mandarin shidaiqu (Shanghai jazz-pop) and the Pathé seven-great-singing-stars era of the 1930s-40s. Electrical disc-cut to shellac, live small-orchestra tracking. Distinct from the post-1949 mainland Chinese recording context.

name: Tokyo major-label studio (CBS Sony / Victor 1970s-80s)
note: Tokyo flagship major-label studios from the late 1970s onward — CBS Sony Roppongi Studio, Victor Aoyama, Sound City, Polystar — where the city-pop canon, classic enka, kayokyoku idol-pop, and J-pop crossover were tracked. Studer A800/A820, SSL/MCI/Neve consoles, full Western mainstream gear. Indistinguishable from Western flagships by gear; the distinction is repertoire and production-school.

name: Hong Kong cantopop studio (PolyGram / Capital Artists 1980s)
note: Hong Kong cantopop studio context — PolyGram Hong Kong, Capital Artists, Bonbon Studio — the infrastructure for the cantopop vocal canon of the 1980s. Soundcraft/SSL/Studer kit. Distinct from Tokyo mainstream by repertoire (Cantonese vs Japanese) and by tighter, drier mix aesthetic.

name: Korean gugak hall (National Gugak Center class)
note: Korean gugak performance and recording halls — the National Gugak Center (Seoul, Busan, Namwon) and similar academic and broadcast facilities. Wood-and-stone modern architecture with traditional Korean aesthetic; medium natural decay suitable for jeongak court music, minsogak folk forms, sanjo, pansori. KBS Classical Music traditional broadcasts trace here. Distinct from Western classical concert halls.

name: Estudios Areíto / EGREM Havana (1962–present)
note: Estudios Areíto in Havana, established 1944 as Panart, nationalized 1961 and operated since by EGREM (the Cuban state recording enterprise). The room is a converted 1930s mansion with high ceiling and wood floor. Tracking context for the post-revolutionary dance-band canon, the timba canon, and the 1996 international son-revival sessions. The defining post-1962 Cuban canon was tracked here. Distinct from pre-revolutionary Panart-era recording at the same address but with US gear and US distribution.

name: Panart / Puchito / RCA Cuba pre-revolutionary Havana (1944–1960)
note: Pre-revolutionary Havana commercial studios — Panart (founded 1944), Puchito (1954), RCA Victor de Cuba, and Velvet de Cuba — that tracked the classic son cubano, mambo, cha-cha-chá, danzón, and bolero canon. US-aligned gear (RCA mics, Ampex tape, Western Electric consoles) and US distribution channels. Panart became the nucleus of EGREM after 1961 nationalization.

name: Havana solar courtyard (rumba outdoor folkloric)
note: Havana solar (tenement courtyard) — the originating context for rumba folkloric in its three subforms (yambú, guaguancó, columbia). Stone-paved central patio surrounded by tenement walls 2-3 stories tall, creating slap-back from hard surfaces. Three congas (quinto-lead, tres-golpes, tumbadora) plus claves, palitos (sticks-on-wood), and a circle of clappers and singers. Smithsonian Folkways field recordings and the Matanzas rumba groups trace here.

name: Fania / La Tierra / Good Vibrations NY studios (1968-1977)
note: Fania-era New York studios — La Tierra (Manhattan), Good Vibrations (NYC), Mediasound, Bell Sound — where the Fania catalog was tracked 1968-1977. Live multi-mic tracking of horn section, piano, congas/bongos/timbales, bass, lead vocals. Mid-tier American Neve/MCI-class consoles, 16-then-24-track 2-inch tape. Distinct from the Cuban Areíto context: NY production aesthetic, US gear, US distribution. The defining salsa nuyorican canon traces here.

name: Odeon / RCA Victor Argentina Buenos Aires (1920s-1960s)
note: Odeon Buenos Aires (two central-city locations) and RCA Victor Argentina — the recording infrastructure for the Argentine tango canon from the 1917-1935 singer era through the orquesta típica golden age and into the later quintet era. Large live tracking rooms suited to a 12-piece orquesta típica (4 bandoneons, 4 violins, piano, bass, sometimes singer). Pre-electrical disc-cut transitioning to tape ~1948.

name: Mexico City Peerless / Musart / RCA Mexicana (1950s-60s)
note: Mexico City flagship major-label studios — Discos Peerless (founded 1934, Mexican-owned), Discos Musart, RCA Victor Mexicana, Columbia Mexicana — that tracked the canon of ranchera, bolero ranchero, corrido, and orchestrated mariachi. US-pattern gear (RCA condensers, Ampex tape, Western Electric consoles). Distinct from the outdoor mariachi tradition at Plaza Garibaldi.

name: Plaza Garibaldi outdoor (Mexico City mariachi tradicional)
note: Plaza Garibaldi (Mexico City) — the historical outdoor gathering point for mariachi groups soliciting work, where mariachi tradicional has been performed and (occasionally) field-recorded since the early 20th century. Open-air stone-paved plaza surrounded by 19th-century buildings. The mariachi vihuela, guitarrón, two violins, two trumpets standard ensemble formed here. Distinct from the studio mariachi context which became dominant after 1950.

name: Discos Fuentes Medellín (1934-onward, Colombian Caribbean canon)
note: Discos Fuentes (founded 1934 in Cartagena, later moved to Medellín) — the Colombian major label and recording infrastructure for cumbia, porro, vallenato, and Colombian-Caribbean tropical music, including the early vallenato canon. US-pattern gear, live-tracking aesthetic. Codiscos (Medellín, 1950s-onward) is the sibling major.

name: Andean altiplano outdoor (huayno / sikuri field context)
note: Andean altiplano (high-plateau Bolivia/Peru, 3000-4000m altitude) outdoor context for huayno (Quechua), sikuri (Aymara), morenada, kullahuada, and other Andean musics. High-altitude thin-air acoustic affects voice and wind-instrument timbre. Field-recording context for the Smithsonian Folkways Andean canon. Distinct from any indoor studio.

name: Santo Domingo / Karen Records / Kubaney studio (1970s-80s)
note: Dominican Republic flagship studio context — Karen Records (Santo Domingo), Kubaney Records (Miami, Dominican-diaspora), Discos Bartolo — that tracked the merengue dominicano canon and the bachata canon (through the crossover era). Mid-tier American gear, live-band tracking through the 1980s, DAW from the 1990s.

name: Englewood Cliffs cedar-vaulted jazz studio NJ (1959-2016)
note: Purpose-built engineer-owned studio in Englewood Cliffs, NJ, designed with an architect and opened July 1959 after the move from a Hackensack living room. The defining American jazz recording room from 1959 onward — Blue Note, Prestige (until 1959), Impulse! (the December 1964 and June 1965 landmarks), and CTI sessions tracked here. Signature workflow: three-mic purist setup, custom-modified RCA and Neumann electronics, no overdubs. The rooms wood-vaulted ceiling and trapezoidal floor plan created a medium natural reverberation that became the auditory signature of post-bop.

name: Hackensack parents living-room studio NJ (1944-1959)
note: A Hackensack, NJ family living room — converted into a recording studio that its engineer operated nights and weekends from 1944 to 1959. Small low-ceilinged room with absorption treatment the engineer designed himself. The early Blue Note hard bop canon was tracked here (1954-1959). The transition to the Englewood Cliffs purpose-built studio happened in mid-1959.

name: Columbia converted-church studio NYC (1949-1981)
note: Columbia Records flagship recording space in Manhattan — converted from a Greek Orthodox church in 1949, occupying the entire nave with the 100-foot vaulted ceiling intact and hardwood floor. The defining American live-tracking room across genres: the 1959-1960 modal-jazz landmarks, canonical 1955 and 1981 solo-piano recordings, composer-conducted classical sessions, and pop-vocal standards. The churchs vault acoustic gave Columbia jazz sessions a chamber-orchestral spaciousness no other contemporary studio matched. Demolished 1981, building replaced by a parking garage.

name: Plaza Sound at Radio City Music Hall NYC (1949-1980s)
note: Plaza Sound Studios, located on the eighth floor of Radio City Music Hall, NYC. Operated as a commercial studio from 1949 through the mid-1980s. The defining room for the Impulse! Records mid-60s catalog (1961-1966 large-ensemble and live-overdub jazz sessions). Also tracked the 1976 punk-canon debut and many producer-engineered pop sessions. Distinct from the Englewood Cliffs cedar-vaulted jazz studio for its Manhattan-Deco room sound — more reflective, less wood-vaulted.

name: A&R Recording NYC (jazz-vocal engineering flagship, 1958-1990s)
note: A&R Recording, founded 1958 in Manhattan and later moved to a second Midtown location. The defining American studio for jazz vocal and singer-songwriter sessions through its founding engineers work: the 1963 bossa nova crossover canon, mid-60s Reprise vocal sessions, pop-jazz crossover productions, and later 70s-80s singer-songwriter records. Mid-tier American gear (early Neve through 80s SSL).

name: Capitol Records Tower Studios Hollywood (1956-present)
note: The Capitol Records Tower in Hollywood, opened 1956 — the 13-story circular-tower headquarters with three recording studios (A, B, C) on the ground floors and a basement complex of eight echo chambers purpose-designed for Capitol. The defining American major-label jazz-and-pop studio: the 1953-1962 crooner canon, the post-1956 vocal-jazz sessions, and the late-60s easy-jazz canon were tracked here. The echo chambers — engineered concrete-walled subterranean rooms with carefully calculated reverberation times — became the secret signature of Capitols pop sound.

name: Strata-East Records loft / Brooklyn loft jazz (1971-mid-1970s)
note: Strata-East Records, founded 1971 by a trumpeter and a pianist as a musician-owned collective, was the leading independent collective for the early-70s spiritual jazz and loft jazz movement. Tracked at various Manhattan and Brooklyn loft spaces (the artists own apartments or modest rented commercial spaces) with portable Ampex/Scully tape machines and modest gear. Aesthetic distinct from the Englewood Cliffs cedar-vaulted jazz studio: less polished, more documentary, capturing the late-60s/early-70s Black political-spiritual jazz movement.

name: Sunset Sound Recorders Hollywood (1958-present)
note: Sunset Sound Recorders in Hollywood, founded 1958. The defining 60s/70s Los Angeles tracking facility for the 1967-1984 rock and singer-songwriter catalogs. On-site echo chambers, Fender Bassman amp room, and live tracking philosophy with strategic overdub.

name: San Francisco Bay Area rock studio (late-60s/70s flagship, 1969-1980)
note: San Francisco rock studio opened 1969 by a touring remote-recording pioneer who had recorded the major late-60s rock festivals. The defining Bay Area rock studio of the late-60s/70s, tracking the 1970 folk-rock supergroup and SF psychedelic-rock canon. The facility passed to Filmways in 1980 and still operates under a later name.

name: A&M Studios (converted film-studio lot) Hollywood (1966-1999)
note: A&M Studios, Hollywood — the label founders bought a former film-studio lot in 1966 and converted it into their record label headquarters and recording complex. Studio A (large live room), B (medium), C (small), D (vocal). The defining LA flagship for 70s singer-songwriter recording and 80s major pop-rock. Decommissioned 1999; the facility continues as a recording complex under a later name.

name: The Village Recorder West Los Angeles (1968-present)
note: The Village Recorder in West LA — converted from a Masonic temple in 1968, the multi-studio facility (A through D, later E) became the defining late-70s LA major-budget studio. Studio D is one of the largest tracking rooms in LA. Distinct from A and M and Sunset Sound for its larger-budget multi-room flagship scale.

name: Caribou Ranch Studio Colorado (1972-1985)
note: Caribou Ranch Studio on a 4,000-acre ranch near Nederland, Colorado at 8,000 feet altitude — producer-operated 1972-1985. The defining destination-residential studio of the 70s: artists came for weeks-long sessions with full ranch amenities, and a run of major 1972-1980 rock, pop and soul albums was tracked here. Closed after a 1985 fire.

name: Electric Lady Studios NYC (1970-present)
note: Electric Lady Studios in Greenwich Village — built at a cost of one million dollars, opened August 1970. The defining NYC rock-and-indie studio from 1970 onward. Studio A is the large tracking room. A canonical run of 1972-77 soul, punk and art-rock albums and 2010s indie and electronic records was tracked here. Continuous operation from 1970 to present makes it the longest-running NYC flagship.

name: Studio in the Country Bogalusa Louisiana (1973-present)
note: Studio in the Country in Bogalusa, Louisiana — opened 1973 in a rural pine-forest setting an hour north of New Orleans. The defining American destination-residential studio for southern, Gulf Coast, and Americana recording. Live tracking room with the pine-forest natural acoustic as part of the appeal.

name: Takoma home recording — parlor / Berkeley portable Ampex (1959-1975)
note: The defining low-budget recording context for original-era American primitive guitar (1959-1975) — the 100-copy self-pressed 1959 debut was tracked in a parents Takoma Park, Maryland living room with a borrowed portable Ampex tape machine; the early Takoma catalog (through 1965, then the second-wave roster) was tracked in similar parlor / home / modest-Berkeley-studio contexts after the label moved west. Single-mic-or-stereo-pair purist tracking philosophy: solo steel-string fingerstyle guitarist, no overdubs, no compression beyond what the tape itself provided. The recording aesthetic became part of the genre — bright, dry, intimate, with the guitar dominant in the frame.

name: Hexham Head chamber-folk studio (mid-2000s onward, Pennsylvania)
note: Hexham Head studio operated out of a converted Pennsylvania country house from the mid-2000s onward — the defining context for contemporary American folk-noir chamber recording. The room has a small natural-decay live area suited to intimate single-room ensemble tracking — voice, fingerpicked guitar, modest strings and percussion — with characteristic reverb processing on the lead vocal as a defining production gesture.

name: Denver Gothic basement / DIY indie studio (mid-1990s onward)
note: The Denver / Colorado Front Range DIY-indie tracking context for the gothic-Americana scene from the mid-1990s onward. Often basement or modest-warehouse rooms with portable digital multitrack gear, occasional excursion to indie commercial rooms (Glasshouse Recording in Fort Collins) for fuller-band sessions. The defining production aesthetic: distorted hurdy-gurdy or distorted banjo through guitar amplifiers, dry-but-aggressive vocal tracking, Old Testament / Pentecostal lyrical imagery.

name: Stax Records Studio A Memphis (1957-1975)
note: Stax Records Studio A, Memphis — converted from the Capitol movie theatre by the label founders in 1957. The defining Southern soul recording room: the converted theatre kept the sloped floor (sloping toward where the screen had been), giving the room an unusual non-rectangular geometry that became the auditory signature. Everyone tracked in the same room with minimal isolation: the house band plus the horn section plus the vocalist. Closed and demolished 1975 after bankruptcy; replica museum on site since 2003.

name: FAME Studios Muscle Shoals (1959-present)
note: FAME Studios in Muscle Shoals, Alabama — founded 1959 (originally Florence Alabama Music Enterprises). The defining Southern soul tracking room of the 60s, home of the 1967 one-day session that broke a major soul singers commercial career. FAMEs house rhythm section (1959-1969) broke off to start Muscle Shoals Sound Studio.

name: Muscle Shoals Sound Studio (1969-1979)
note: Muscle Shoals Sound Studio, Sheffield, Alabama — opened 1969 by FAMEs former house rhythm section after they broke away from FAME Studios. Converted from a coffin warehouse with a tin roof. The defining American rhythm-section-for-hire studio of the 70s, tracking Southern soul, British and American rock, and singer-songwriter sessions from December 1969 onward.

name: Sigma Sound Studios Philadelphia (1968-2003)
note: Sigma Sound Studios, Philadelphia — founded 1968 by its house engineer. The defining home of the Philadelphia soul sound from 1971 onward, when Philadelphia International Records (PIR) was founded and made Sigma its de facto house studio, with the labels rhythm section tracking here as house band. Distinct from Stax / FAME / Muscle Shoals for its orchestral-pop arrangement aesthetic — live string sections tracked at Sigma, large 12-musician rhythm section, the polished Philly soul sound.

name: Hitsville USA Motown Studio A Detroit (1959-1972, the Snakepit)
note: Hitsville USA, Detroit — the label founder converted a two-story house into Motowns headquarters in 1959, with Studio A occupying what had been the basement at the back. Tiny tracking room (~25 m²) with low ceiling. The defining Northern soul / Motown sound: the house band (bass, drums, piano, two guitars, tambourine) tracked here daily 1959-1972. Three-track tape until 1965, then eight-track. Tambourine on beats 2 and 4 was so foundational that it became known as the Motown backbeat.

name: Atlantic Studios NYC (1947-1976)
note: Atlantic Studios, NYC — the Atlantic Records founders set up the room in the late 1940s, and its house engineer (1947-1975 at Atlantic) made it one of the defining R&B and jazz studios of the 50s and 60s. The pre-1959 jump blues and classic R&B canon was tracked here, along with landmark late-50s modern jazz sessions. The labels later Southern-soul catalog was often tracked at FAME or Muscle Shoals Sound and mixed at Atlantic NYC.

name: King Records Studios Cincinnati (1943-1971)
note: King Records Studios, Cincinnati — founded 1943 as one of the first integrated American record labels. The defining home of the proto-funk and funk canon from 1956 through 1971, including the 1964-1970 landmark sides and the most-sampled drum break of 1970. Distinct from Stax for its smaller-scale indie-commercial aesthetic and its central role in proto-funk rhythmic-displacement vocabulary.

name: Chess Studios Chicago (1957-1975)
note: Chess Studios, Chicago — the label moved to this building in 1957. The defining home of Chicago electric blues and early R&B. The room produced the urban Chicago blues sound — electric-bass-rooted, amplified harmonica through a distorted small amp, Telecaster or Stratocaster lead, snare-with-rim-shot backbeat.

name: Lisbon Alfama fado tavern (Casa de Fados, 1920s onward)
note: The Casa de Fados small tavern in Lisbons Alfama, Bairro Alto, and Mouraria quarters — the canonical context for fado de Lisboa from the 1920s onward through the mid-century commercial recordings and into the modern revival. Small intimate room with stone-and-tile walls, 30-or-fewer seat capacity, the audience sitting silently with lights dimmed during fado performance. Standard ensemble: solo voice (the fadista), guitarra portuguesa (12-string Portuguese guitar), viola de fado (Portuguese classical guitar), occasionally viola baixo (acoustic bass guitar). The room acoustic is dry-but-stone-reflective and intimate.

name: Coimbra university outdoor quad / Sé Velha steps (fado de Coimbra)
note: The Coimbra University quadrangle (Pátio das Escolas), the Sé Velha cathedral steps, and other outdoor stone-paved squares in the historic Coimbra university quarter — canonical context for fado de Coimbra, the academic-male-student fado tradition distinct from the commercial fado de Lisboa lineage. Performed by male student ensembles (often called grupos de fados) wearing the traditional black student cape (capa e batina). Outdoor stone-paved spaces with hard reflective surfaces give the genre its characteristic open-air projection. Distinct from Lisboa fado in vocal register (typically male tenor / baritone), repertoire (university student songs, poetry-set songs), and performance context (outdoor serenata vs intimate tavern).

name: Andalusian flamenco tablao (Seville / Granada / Madrid)
note: The flamenco tablao — small intimate stage venue with stone or tile floor that flamenco bailaores (dancers) zapatear (heel-strike percuss) upon, surrounded by audience seating on three sides. The canonical context for cante jondo (deep song), cante chico (light song), and the full flamenco ensemble of cantaor (singer), guitarrista, bailaor, and palmero (clapper). Found historically in Seville, Granada, Cádiz, Jerez, Madrid (Café de Chinitas in the 1840s onward), and the modern tablao circuit in Spanish tourist quarters. Distinct from concert-hall flamenco (which is theatrical staging) and from peña flamenca (private flamenco-association club) gatherings.

name: Athens / Piraeus rebetadika tekes-and-koutoukia (1920s-1940s)
note: The rebetadika and koutoukia of Piraeus and Athens — small Greek tavern-and-cafe contexts of the 1920s-1940s where rebetiko (Greek urban underclass blues-equivalent) was performed and recorded. After the 1922 Asia Minor Catastrophe brought Greek refugees from Smyrna and other Anatolian cities to Athens, the displaced population concentrated in Piraeus and developed rebetiko as their characteristic music. Standard ensemble: voice, bouzouki (long-neck lute, often four-course tetraxordo until the 1950s six-course conversion), baglamas (small high-pitched bouzouki), guitar, sometimes santouri. Lyrical content concerns hashish, prison, exile, poverty, romantic suffering. Distinct from Athens nightclub laiko (post-1955 commercial extension) and from Smyrna café aman (the original Anatolian source tradition).

name: Athens Minos / Columbia Greece / Lyra studios (1955-1985)
note: The major Athens record-label studios from 1955 onward — Minos Records, Columbia Greece, Lyra Records, His Masters Voice Greece — that tracked the post-rebetiko Greek popular music canon. Three principal genres tracked here: laiko (commercial nightclub bouzouki music, the electrified-bouzouki era), éntechno (literary art-song setting Greek poetry to music by the canonical mid-century composers), and elafro (light orchestrated Greek pop). Live tracking room, modest mid-tier European gear (Telefunken / EMI), tape 15ips. Distinct from the rebetadika (informal tavern recording) of the 1930s-1940s.

name: Mount Athos Byzantine monastery chant context
note: The katholikon (main church) of Mount Athos Greek Orthodox monasteries — the canonical context for Byzantine liturgical chant, which has continued in unbroken practice since the 9th century. Stone-walled architecture with medium-to-long natural decay (1.5-3 seconds). Standard practice: ison (sustained drone note held by chorus) with melismatic chanter (psaltis) carrying the melody on top, no harmonization, no instruments. The eight-mode oktoechos modal system governs the modal-rotation across the liturgical year. Distinct from Anglican / Roman Catholic Western choral practice (which uses harmony) and from Russian Orthodox chant (which has its own modal-and-harmonic vocabulary).

name: Prague Supraphon Mozarteum studio (1948-onward, Czech national label)
note: Supraphon studios in Prague — the Czech state record label (founded 1932 as Esta Records, nationalized 1948 as Supraphon) with its principal Mozarteum studio. The defining Czech / Czechoslovak studio for classical (Czech Philharmonic), folk-revival, written-poetry song-setting (písnička), and pop. Live tracking room, modest mid-tier European gear (Tesla / Telefunken), tape 15ips through 1990 then DAW. Tracked the Czech singer-songwriter, underground-rock (clandestinely), and broader written-poetry-song tradition.

name: Warsaw Polskie Nagrania Muza studios (1956-1990)
note: Polskie Nagrania Muza studios in Warsaw — the Polish state record label (founded 1956) and principal recording infrastructure for Polish popular music, folk, classical, and the distinctive Polish poezja śpiewana (sung-poetry) tradition that set the work of Polish poets to music. Live tracking room, modest mid-tier European gear (Tesla / Tonsil), tape 15ips. Distinct from Poljazz (separate Polish jazz label).

name: Irish pub session room (Doolin / Clare / Galway 1970s-onward)
note: The small wooden-paneled pub session room — the Doolin pubs, the Galway city session pubs, and countless other Clare / Galway / Donegal / West Cork pubs — that became the canonical context for the Irish trad session revival from the 1970s onward following the 1970s folk-revival ensemble rediscovery. Small intimate room with turf or peat-fire corner, session table arranged in a tight circle, all instruments acoustic and unamplified. Standard ensemble: fiddle, tin whistle, flute, bodhrán, sometimes uilleann pipes or concertina, accordion, harp, and bouzouki added in the post-revival era. Distinct from concert-hall Irish trad (which is staged performance) and from RTÉ studio Irish trad (which is broadcast-engineered).

name: Connemara / Donegal kitchen sean-nós context
note: The Gaeltacht kitchen — the canonical context for sean-nós (old-style) unaccompanied Irish-Gaelic-language solo singing. Performed in Connemara (Conamara), Donegal (Dún na nGall), and West Kerry (Corca Dhuibhne) Gaeltacht regions where Irish remains a living vernacular. Standard practice: solo voice, unaccompanied, melismatic ornamental style varying by regional school (Connemara is more melismatic, Donegal more straight-toned, Munster intermediate). Repertoire includes laments, lullabies, working songs, love songs, and narrative ballads in the Irish language. Performance context historically was a kitchen gathering with the singer seated and a friend or neighbor holding the singers hand as encouragement. Distinct from Irish-language song with instrumental accompaniment.

name: UK folk-revival club circuit (London Soho / Newcastle / Manchester 1960s-70s)
note: The British folk-revival club circuit of the late-1950s through mid-1980s — Les Cousins in Soho, the Troubadour in Earls Court, the Bridge Folk Club in Newcastle, the King and Queen in Bloomsbury, and a network of similar small 50-100-capacity clubs where the British folk revival was performed and codified. Standard ensemble: solo voice + acoustic guitar, or solo voice unaccompanied, or full-band reconstructions. Repertoire drew heavily on the early-20th-century field-collected canon, the classic ballad corpus, and the radical revival reconstructions. Distinct from Greenwich Village confessional (which is American singer-songwriter songcraft) and from the Irish trad session (which is instrumental tunes-not-songs centered).

name: Scottish bothy farmhouse kitchen (Aberdeenshire Doric tradition)
note: The Aberdeenshire farmhouse bothy — the small farm-cottage building where male agricultural workers (bothy boys) lived during seasonal employment from the 19th through mid-20th centuries — was the originating context for the bothy ballad tradition, sung in Doric Scots dialect. Standard practice: unaccompanied solo voice or small group, narrative ballad with verse-and-chorus structure, often humorous-satirical content about farm life. The Greentrax / Topic Records field-recording canon (Hamish Henderson, the School of Scottish Studies) captured the tradition in its declining mid-20th-century form. Distinct from Highland Scottish Gaelic song (which uses different repertoire and language) and from Lowland Scots ballad-revival (which is performed-recreated rather than living-tradition).

name: Cajun French Louisiana dance hall (Lafayette / Eunice / Mamou 1940s-onward)
note: The South Louisiana Cajun French dance hall (fais do-do) — the Breaux Bridge dance halls, the Liberty Theater in Eunice (Saturday morning live Cajun radio show), the Eunice music-store jam rooms, the Mamou dance-hall bars — the canonical context for Cajun French music from the 1930s onward following the commercial-recording era and the post-WWII dance-hall revival. Wooden dance-floor context with standard ensemble: Cajun single-row diatonic accordion (LeBlanc / Acadian / Bon Cajun makes), Cajun fiddle (specific tuning and ornamentation), guitar, occasionally upright bass and a single triangle. Two-step and waltz the dominant dances. Distinct from zydeco (Black Creole French Louisiana with washboard / rubboard frottoir percussion) and from Texas Czech / German polka dance halls.

name: Berlin Kabarett / Liedermacher song-cabaret studio (1920s and 1970s onward)
note: The Berlin / Munich Kabarett and Liedermacher song-cabaret context — Weimar-era roots (the Schall und Rauch cabaret, the 1920s composer-playwright song-theater collaborations) extended through the post-1968 Liedermacher revival (including the Ostdeutscher Liedermacher tradition under GDR repression). Standard ensemble: solo voice with piano or acoustic guitar or accordion accompaniment, lyrical content politically and literarily engaged, performance context the literarisches Kabarett (literary cabaret) with intimate seated audience and an explicitly intellectual register distinct from commercial Schlager pop.

name: Bulgarian State Radio hall Sofia (1952-onward, female-choir polyphony context)
note: The Bulgarian State Radio hall in Sofia — recording context for the state folk ensemble (founded 1952) and the state broadcasters female vocal choir, whose 1975 Nonesuch Explorer release made Bulgarian female-choir polyphony internationally famous. Large hall with medium-long natural decay. Repertoire: Bulgarian village folk-song repertoire (Rhodope and Pirin regional traditions) reharmonized for concert-stage female chorus by the ensembles composer-arrangers.

name: Norwegian Hardanger fjord outdoor / barn context
note: The Hardangerfjord (western Norway) outdoor and barn-context home of the Hardanger fiddle (hardingfele) — the regional Norwegian violin variant with four playing strings and four-or-five sympathetic resonance strings below the fingerboard. Performed solo for traditional dance forms (springar, gangar, halling, pols) at weddings and seasonal celebrations in outdoor and stabbur (storehouse) contexts across western Norway.

name: Sápmi outdoor tundra / lavvu context (Sámi yoik)
note: The Sápmi (Sámi cultural region spanning northern Norway, Sweden, Finland, and Russia) arctic tundra and lavvu (Sámi traditional tent) outdoor context for the Sámi yoik (luohti / juoiggus, varying by Sámi language) — the unique Sámi vocal tradition of singing-about rather than singing-of (a yoik does not have a subject, it IS its subject — a person, an animal, a place). Often performed solo without accompaniment, sometimes with sálldi frame drum.

name: Moscow Melodiya state studio (1964-1991, then 1991-onward)
note: Melodiya — the USSR (1964-1991) and Russian Federation state recording label and its principal Moscow recording studio. The canonical home of nearly all Soviet-era Russian recording: classical (the great Soviet piano, violin and cello soloists), estrada (Soviet light pop), bardic song / avtorskaya pesnya, Soviet rock, Russian folk-revival (state folk choirs, Russian folk balalaika ensembles, byliny narrative recitations).

name: Klezmer simcha celebration hall (Eastern European Jewish wedding context)
note: The simcha (Yiddish for celebration) hall — the wedding / Bar Mitzvah / brit milah / holiday celebration context for traditional Eastern European Ashkenazi Jewish klezmer music. Standard klezmer ensemble: clarinet, violin, accordion or bayan, bass, tsimbl (hammered dulcimer). Revival from the 1970s onward through the klezmer-revival ensembles. Separate but kindred tradition: the synagogue-context cantorial khazonus tradition.

name: Budapest / Carpathian csárda tavern (Hungarian and Romanian taraf context)
note: The csárda — Hungarian and Romanian-Hungarian roadside tavern that became the canonical context for Romani tavern music across the Carpathian Basin from the 18th century onward. Standard ensemble: primás (lead violin), kontra (second violin or viola), bass (cello or bőgő bass), cimbalom (concert-pedal large hammered dulcimer). The Hungarian-Romani repertoire crosses Hungarian csárdás dance, Hungarian art-music (the 19th-century Hungarian-dance and rhapsody repertoire). In Romania, the related taraf tradition shares the same cimbalom-and-violin foundation with smaller portable ţambal.

name: Decca West African studios (Lagos / Accra 1947-1975)
note: Decca West Africa (Lagos, Nigeria, opened 1947; Accra, Ghana, opened 1953) — the British Decca Records subsidiary that produced the first commercial recordings of West African popular music canon. Tracked the early Highlife canon and the early Juju canon on 78 rpm shellac and later 7-inch vinyl. Live-band one-or-two-take sessions with full ensemble (guitars, percussion battery, horn section, voice all in one room). Distinct from the post-1965 EMI Lagos / Phonogram Lagos era which had multitrack capability.

name: Kinshasa / Brazzaville Congolese studios (1953-onward, Congolese rumba canon)
note: The Kinshasa (formerly Léopoldville) and Brazzaville recording studios that tracked the Congolese rumba / soukous canon from 1953 onward, when the founding rival orchestras formed; the 1960 independence-era landmark sides tracked here. Later studios: IAD Kinshasa, Veve Records. Distinct from Paris Pathé-Marconi / Sonima studios where Congolese music was tracked for European distribution from the 1970s onward.

name: Paris Pathé-Marconi / Sonima / Studio Marcadet (1970s-1990s Francophone African diaspora)
note: The Paris recording studios that tracked the Francophone African diaspora music canon from the 1970s onward — Pathé-Marconi EMI France in Boulogne-Billancourt, Sonima Studios, Studio Marcadet (the canonical small Paris room for the Lusafrica catalog), Studio Davout. Most major Francophone African artists tracked in Paris during their commercial peak (1972-1992). Studio recording infrastructure superior to most contemporaneous African studios, with continued artist-and-producer connection to home country recording context.

name: Johannesburg Gallo African Studios (1932-onward, all SA canon)
note: The Johannesburg Gallo African Studios, South Africa — opened 1932, the canonical home of all major South African 20th-century commercial recording: pre-apartheid jazz, the mbube vocal-group tradition (from the 1939 recording that later became a global pop standard after a tortured rights-acquisition history), isicathamiya choral tradition (from 1973 onward), mbaqanga, kwela penny-whistle 1950s street music, the entire 1960s-70s township pop catalog, kwaito 1990s post-apartheid, and modern amapiano / SA hip-hop crossover. Distinct from the parallel SABC (state broadcaster) studio infrastructure.

name: Dar es Salaam / Zanzibar taarab culture-club (1905-onward)
note: The taarab culture-club room of Zanzibar Stone Town and Dar es Salaam — the canonical context for taarab music, the Swahili coastal East African genre that fuses Arab maqam-system melody, Indian classical raga vocabulary, and Bantu-Swahili language poetry into ensemble-with-orchestra performance for weddings and celebrations. Standard ensemble: large orchestra of 15-30 musicians including violin section, oud, qanun, accordion, ney, harmonium, riq tambourine, dumbak. The Zanzibar tradition was codified through the first commercial recording star of East African music (recorded by HMV in Bombay in 1928), a long-lived taarab matriarch (1910-2013), and the Stone Town culture-club orchestras (a flagship club founded 1958).

name: Harare / Salisbury Zimbabwean studios (1970s-onward, chimurenga and Zimbabwean pop)
note: The Harare (named Salisbury until 1982) recording studios that tracked the chimurenga (Zimbabwean liberation-struggle music) canon and the broader Zimbabwean pop. Chimurenga was codified from 1973 onward — translating Shona mbira repertoire into the electric-band context with electric guitars playing mbira interlocking-cycle patterns (kushaura and kutsinhira), against the Lion Records and Gramma Records studio infrastructure. Continued through the Zimbabwean rumba / pop hybrid at Pakare Paye. Distinct from the Bulawayo regional Ndebele-tradition recording context.

name: Bamako / Kayes Mande griot (jeli) compound (timeless, courtyard tradition)
note: The Mande jeli (griot, in the Portuguese-derived European exonym) compound courtyard — the canonical traditional context for the Mande hereditary praise-singer caste tradition spanning Mali, Guinea, Senegal, Burkina Faso, Gambia. Standard jeli ensemble: kora (21-string harp-lute, plucked by men of the Kouyaté / Cissokho / Diabaté griot lineages), ngoni (small lute, the ancestor of the American banjo), balafon (gourd-resonated xylophone tuned to the seven-near-equal-division Mande heptatonic), tama (small armpit-pressed talking drum), djembe (Maninka goblet drum), and voice. The Kela village in Mali is the historical anchor of the Sundiata Keita Sosso-bala epic recitation tradition. Compound performance context is outdoor courtyard, with the jeli providing genealogical praise-poetry for noble patrons.

name: Cairo Studio Misr / Sono Cairo (1934-onward, golden-age tarab era)
note: The major Cairo recording studios that tracked the Egyptian classical tarab canon — Studio Misr (founded 1934 as part of the broader Misr industrial-cultural project to develop Egyptian sovereign cultural infrastructure), Sono Cairo, and the later Cairo Radio studios. The defining home of the canonical 20th-century Arab vocalists and composer-singers: weekly Thursday-night live-broadcast concerts from Cairo from 1937 onward, enormous song-form takhts of 30-60 minutes per piece, the modernized Egyptian classical idiom, and the post-WWII romantic crooner style. Large tracking-room capacity (the full Arabic orchestra of 30-50 musicians — violin section, oud, qanun, ney, riq, darbuka, accordion, cello, double bass), period-appropriate European gear adapted to the larger ensemble size.

name: Tehran Persian classical dastgāh context (Conservatoire Studios + private salons)
note: The Tehran Conservatoire (Honarestan-e Musiqi-ye Melli, founded 1907) studios and the private aristocratic salon context that produced the canonical recordings of Persian classical dastgāh in the pre-1979 era. The defining masters of voice, tar, kamancheh, and santur tracked here. Standard ensemble: solo voice plus avaz (free-meter vocal improvisation) accompanied by tar and/or setar and/or santur and/or kamancheh, with tombak frame-drum providing rhythmic foundation when metric sections (chaharmezrab, reng, kereshmeh) appear. Small intimate ensemble (3-6 musicians), master-disciple transmission context. Distinct from post-1979 Iranian pop recording and from the Tehrangeles Persian-pop diaspora.

name: Istanbul makam classical and arabesk studio (Plak / Kervan / Türkofon labels 1955-onward)
note: The major Istanbul recording studios from 1955 onward that tracked the Turkish classical makam, arabesk, and anadolu rock canons — Türkofon, Plak, Kervan, Şah Plak, Coşkun Plak, the labels of the Beyoğlu / Galata / Üsküdar studio circuit. The defining classical Turkish makam canon: the mid-century Turkish Art Music concert singers. The arabesk canon — the Turkish-Egyptian-musical-fusion popular genre that dominated Turkish mass culture from the 1970s-90s, set against urban-rural migration anxiety. Anadolu rock also tracked here in the late 1960s-70s before Turkish rock studios diversified.

name: Baghdad Iraqi maqam context (chalghi ensemble at private and broadcast studios 1932-2003)
note: The Baghdad recording context for Iraqi maqam (al-Maqam al-Iraqi) — the distinctive Iraqi classical vocal tradition that pairs a solo qari (vocalist) reciting Arabic poetry in elaborated maqam vocal-form with the small chalghi (or jalghi) ensemble of santur (Iraqi hammered dulcimer, the dominant instrument), jawza (small Iraqi bowed lute), tabla (Iraqi single-headed drum), and riq tambourine. Tracked at private studios and the Al-Baghdadiya / Iraq State Radio studios from 1932 onward through the canonical early-20th-century, post-WWII, and later qari lineage. Distinct from broader Arabic tarab (the Egyptian-Levantine-Syrian classical tradition) — Iraqi maqam has its own specific repertoire (the 56 canonical maqams of the Baghdadi school) and its own canonical instrument battery centered on the santur rather than the oud-and-qanun typical of Egyptian tarab.

name: Fez / Tetouan Andalusi palace and riad context (Andalusī nūba and malhun)
note: The Fez (Fes) and Tetouan palace and riad (traditional Moroccan house with central courtyard) context — the canonical home of the Moroccan Andalusī nūba tradition (also called al-ala or musique andalouse), the classical music tradition that descends from the 11-12th century cultural heritage of Muslim-ruled Iberian Andalusia, brought to North Africa with the post-1492 Iberian Muslim and Jewish expulsion and preserved in Fez, Tetouan, Tangier, Rabat. The 11-nūba cycle (each nūba is a multi-section suite in a single mode lasting 4-7 hours when performed complete) survives in Morocco; the related Algerian gharnati and Tunisian malouf traditions are sister lineages of the same Andalusi root. Standard ensemble: rabab (medieval Andalusi-derived bowed lute), oud, kamenjah (violin held vertically on the knee in Andalusi posture), tar (square frame drum), darbuka, voice. The parallel Maghrebi malhun popular poetic-singing tradition (originating in 16th-century Tafilalt) tracks the same palace-and-riad performance context.

name: Casablanca / Marrakech Moroccan chaabi popular studios (1970s-onward)
note: The Casablanca and Marrakech recording studios that tracked the Moroccan chaabi popular music canon from the 1970s onward, including the raï-crossover generation. The chaabi tradition is the Moroccan-Arabic-language popular wedding-and-celebration music built on the rural Moroccan dance rhythms (haoussa from Casablanca, aita from the Atlantic plains, houara from the Souss valley) with the urban ensemble of oud, violin, banjo (the Moroccan banjo is a Moroccan invention from the late 1960s), darbuka, voice. Distinct from the Algerian raï tradition (which has a parallel but distinct development) and from the Egyptian shaabi (which has Egyptian-Arabic-language and Egyptian rhythmic basis).

name: Yerevan Armenian Komitas conservatoire context (1923-onward)
note: The Yerevan State Conservatory context — founded 1923 to preserve the work of the founding ethnomusicologist of Armenian musical scholarship (1869-1935), who codified the Armenian folk-song corpus before his deportation and breakdown during the 1915 Armenian Genocide. The canonical Yerevan-conservatoire recording infrastructure tracks the Armenian Apostolic Christian liturgical tradition (the sharakan hymn repertoire dating to the 5th-century alphabet creation), the Armenian ashugh secular-poetry-song tradition (the canonical 18th-century three-language Armenian/Georgian/Azeri ashugh repertoire), the duduk (Armenian double-reed apricot-wood pipe) solo tradition, and the modern Armenian folk-revival lineage (duduk and piano).

name: Kolkata HMV Dum Dum studio (1928-onward, the Gramophone Company of India)
note: The HMV Dum Dum studio in Kolkata — the Gramophone Company of India operating since 1928 (originally as the Eastern subsidiary of EMI). The dominant recording infrastructure for Indian classical music for most of the 20th century: Kirana gharana Hindustani vocal, sitar, shehnai, sarod, bansuri, the Carnatic vocal canon, the entire Bengali Rabindra Sangeet tradition, and the early Hindi-film playback singing canon. Large tracking-room orchestra-capable rooms, period-appropriate gear, gradually upgrading from shellac 78 to LP to digital across the 20th century.

name: Mumbai / Bombay filmi recording studios (1940s-onward, Mehboob / Famous playback context)
note: The Mumbai (Bombay) filmi recording studios — Mehboob Studio (founded 1954), Famous Studios (Tardeo, founded 1948), Empire Studios, Film Centre Tardeo, Rang Mahal — the canonical recording infrastructure for the Hindi-language Bollywood film-song playback tradition from the 1940s onward. The defining filmi music-direction lineage: the 1940s-50s orchestrated-classical-folk-fusion template, the 1950s-60s golden age, the 1970s funk-and-bossa-and-disco-fusion era, the Tamil filmi parallel canon, and the 1990s-onward global breakthrough. Large tracking-room orchestra-capable rooms for the characteristic Bollywood orchestral arrangements (50-100 musicians on classical-era recordings).

name: Chennai Music Academy sabha context (1928-onward Carnatic concert tradition)
note: The Chennai (formerly Madras) Music Academy sabha and the broader Chennai sabha-network — Krishna Gana Sabha, Narada Gana Sabha, Sri Parthasarathy Swami Sabha, Sri Krishna Gana Sabha — the canonical concert context for Carnatic classical music from 1928 onward. Large rectangular hall with proscenium-style stage and audience seating, medium-to-long natural decay (1-2 seconds), the annual December Music Season (Margazhi Maha Utsavam, December-January) bringing the entire Carnatic concert world to Chennai for 3-4 weeks of overlapping daily kutcheri concerts. Standard Carnatic kutcheri ensemble: voice or single melodic-instrument soloist (vocalist, violinist, flutist, or veena player) + violin accompanist + mridangam + secondary percussion (ghatam, kanjira, or morsing), with tanpura drone foundation.

name: Varanasi / Benares gharana baithak (Hindustani classical salon context)
note: The Varanasi (Benares) gharana baithak — the canonical intimate small-room salon context for Hindustani classical music performance and master-disciple transmission. Varanasi has been one of the principal Hindustani classical gharana cities for centuries (Benares gharana of tabla, the Atrauli-Jaipur and Benares vocal gharanas) along with Gwalior, Agra, Kirana, Patiala, and Indore. The baithak (literally seated gathering) is a small intimate room with floor-seating, the musician(s) seated on a raised platform, and an audience of 15-30 connoisseurs (rasikas) who follow the elaborated raga performance for the standard 2-3 hour Hindustani concert duration. Standard ensemble: solo vocalist or single-instrument soloist with tabla accompanist, sarangi or harmonium accompanist, and tanpura drone.

name: Vrindavan / Braj mandir bhajan context (Krishna devotional)
note: The Vrindavan / Mathura / Braj region mandir (temple) bhajan context — the canonical home of the Krishna devotional song tradition centered on the Braj region of Uttar Pradesh (the legendary childhood-and-youth landscape of Krishna in Hindu mythology). Temples like Banke Bihari Mandir, Radha Vallabh Mandir, and the broader haveli-sangeet tradition (temple-courtyard musical worship) preserve the Krishna-devotional bhajan corpus in Braj Bhasha, Sanskrit, and Hindi languages. The Pushti Marg tradition of haveli sangeet uses pakhawaj (barrel drum) accompaniment rather than tabla. Distinct from the Vaishnava kirtan tradition (which is more West Bengal centered, congregational call-and-response).

name: Golden Temple Amritsar gurdwara (Harmandir Sahib Sikh Gurmat Sangeet)
note: Harmandir Sahib (the Golden Temple) in Amritsar — the holiest gurdwara of the Sikh religion, where the canonical Sikh Gurmat Sangeet (sacred music of the Gurus) tradition has been performed continuously since the 1604 installation of the Adi Granth scripture by Guru Arjan Dev. The Sikh devotional tradition is built on shabad kirtan (singing of the verses of the Guru Granth Sahib scripture), organized by raga across 31 ragas mentioned in the Granth, performed by trained ragis at the Harmandir Sahib and at gurdwaras worldwide. Traditional Sikh instruments include rabab (Mardanas medieval instrument), saranda, taus (peacock-shaped bowed lute), and dilruba; modern Sikh kirtan typically uses harmonium and tabla.

name: Punjab village bhangra dhol outdoor (harvest celebration context)
note: The Punjab village outdoor harvest-celebration context — the originating performance setting for bhangra, the male-line Punjabi harvest dance and celebration music tradition that was originally performed by farmer-dancers at the Baisakhi (April harvest festival) celebrations across the Punjab region of South Asia (now split between Indian Punjab and Pakistani Punjab). Built on the dhol (large double-headed barrel drum) lead, with the accompanying singers calling out boli (improvised vocal couplets). The post-1980s British-Asian diaspora revival (the Sangeeta and Multitone label catalogs) extended bhangra into the urban-electronic-pop format that has become the global bhangra identifier.

name: Studio One Kingston (1959-2004)
note: Studio One Records, Kingston, Jamaica — founded 1959, the canonical Jamaican recording studio whose catalogue is often called the Motown of Jamaica. The resident house band lineage moved through the 1962-1965 ska era, mid-late 60s rocksteady, 1968-71 early reggae, and the 1970s roots era. Foundational ska, rocksteady and roots-reggae sides from 1964 onward.

name: Waterhouse dub mixing workshop Kingston (1968-1989)
note: The Waterhouse-district Kingston home workshop (1968-1989) — the converted bedroom mixing room where dub was invented in the late 1960s through 1970s. Equipment: 4-track MCI mixer with custom modifications, Roland Space Echo RE-201 tape delay, EMT plate reverb, Mu-Tron biphase phaser, Pultec EQ. Working method: take the rhythm tracks (riddims) tracked at Channel One or Studio One, then perform live re-mixing in real time, dropping voice and instruments in and out, applying tape echo and spring reverb to fragments. The workshops protege lineage carried the method forward through the 1980s.

name: Channel One Studios Kingston (1972-1985, roots-reggae house-band room)
note: Channel One Studios, Kingston — founded 1972. The defining late-70s Jamaican roots-reggae studio, with a resident house band anchored by the drum-and-bass rhythm section that became the most-recorded in reggae history. Foundational roots-reggae vocal-group recordings from 1976 onward, and the early dancehall pivot of the late 70s.

name: Port-au-Prince Haitian kompa studio (Mini Records / Marc Records 1970s-1990s)
note: The Port-au-Prince recording studios that tracked the Haitian kompa-direkt canon from the 1970s onward — Mini Records (founded 1968, the canonical kompa label), Marc Records, Macaya, Geronimo. The defining kompa lineage: the 1955 invention of kompa-direkt, the parallel cadence-rampa lineage, then the post-1970 second-generation Haitian bands — performing in Haitian Creole and French.

name: Trinidad calypso panyard / Carnival mas-camp (community context)
note: The Trinidad and Tobago calypso panyard and Carnival mas-camp — the outdoor community context for calypso (the Trinidadian narrative-and-topical song tradition that emerged from post-1834 Emancipation kalinda stick-fighting chant) and steelband pan music (the Trinidadian steel-drum tradition invented in the late 1930s from oil-drum scavenge). The Carnival mas-camp is the seasonal preparation space (October-February) for Carnival Monday-Tuesday performance; the panyard is the year-round practice space of each steelband. Soca (soul-of-calypso, codified in 1973) extended calypso into faster dance-floor format.

name: Haitian vodou lakou outdoor peristyle (compound ceremony context)
note: The Haitian vodou lakou (family compound) outdoor peristyle (covered ceremonial space) — the canonical context for traditional Haitian vodou ceremonial music. Three principal drum-batteries (the rhythms governing the spirit-pantheon they call): asoto (West African Yoruba-derived), rada (Dahomeyan-derived, calmer spirits), petwo (Kreyol-Haitian innovation, hot fierce spirits). The drum battery is led by the maman tanbou, with the segond tanbou, boula, and ogan iron bell providing the standard four-drum-and-bell rhythmic foundation. Manbo (priestess) or houngan (priest) leads the ceremony with songs (chante vodou) summoning the lwa (spirits) to mount worshippers in trance possession.

name: Brixton / London UK lovers rock basement studio (1976-1985)
note: The Brixton, Acton, Tooting and broader London Black British-Caribbean diaspora basement-studio context — the canonical home of lovers rock, the soft soul-influenced female-vocal-led reggae subgenre that emerged in the UK from 1976 onward as a Black British response to Jamaican roots-reggae. Codified through the founding 1975 lovers rock recording, the 1979 #2 UK chart breakthrough, and a small circle of female vocalists and basement production teams.

name: UK 70s hard rock / progressive / NWOBHM arena studio (Olympic / Trident / Sarm 1968-1985)
note: The major London Class-A commercial studios where the canonical UK hard rock, progressive rock, glam rock, and NWOBHM catalogs were tracked across 1968-1985 — Olympic Studios Barnes, Trident Studios Soho, AIR Studios Oxford Circus, Sarm West Studios Notting Hill, Morgan Studios Willesden. Large tracking-room amplifier-stack capacity, full-band live-tracking with significant isolation, classic-tube-and-transformer signal chains (Neve / Helios consoles, Studer A80 tape).

name: Seattle Reciprocal Recording / Bear Creek grunge studios (1986-1995)
note: The Seattle indie-commercial recording studios that tracked the canonical grunge canon from the late 1980s through the mid 1990s — Reciprocal Recording (the Sub Pop flagship studio, 1987-1989 debut-album sessions), Bear Creek Studio Woodinville WA, London Bridge Studio Shoreline WA (1990-1991 major-label breakthrough sessions). Live-band one-or-two-take session aesthetic, cinder-block-walled tracking rooms, modest-tier indie-commercial signal chains.

name: Stoner / doom / sludge / post-metal amplifier-garage studio (Electrical Audio + scattered amplifier-worshipping rooms)
note: The amplifier-worshipping medium-large tracking-room studios that tracked the canonical stoner / doom / sludge / post-metal canon from the late 1980s onward — Electrical Audio Chicago (1993-2005 canonical sludge and post-metal sessions), Soma Electronic Music Studios Chicago, Sound City Van Nuys (1992-1994 stoner-metal foundational sessions), and a broader scattered network of amplifier-worshipping rooms. Common to all: tracking philosophy that lets the amplifier rig dominate the sound rather than processing-after-the-fact.

name: Gothenburg Swedish melodic death / atmospheric black metal studios (Studio Fredman / Studio Mega 1992-onward)
note: The Gothenburg, Sweden recording studios that tracked the canonical melodic death metal Gothenburg sound from the early 1990s — Studio Fredman (the founding studio of the Gothenburg sound, tracking the landmark 1995-1998 melodic death metal albums), Studio Mega, Abyss Studios. The parallel Norwegian / Scandinavian atmospheric black metal scene (the landmark 1994-1995 albums) was tracked at related Nordic indie-commercial studios.

name: UK shoegaze / dream pop 4AD / Creation studios (1986-1995)
note: The UK 4AD and Creation Records affiliated indie studios where the canonical shoegaze and dream pop canon was tracked across 1986-1995 — Blackwing Studios London, Britannia Row, Protocol, Eden, Trident, Wessex, Falconer (one landmark 1991 album was tracked across 19 different studios over 2 years), Outside Studios, Konk Studios. Standard shoegaze tracking aesthetic: dense wall-of-guitars with reverb / delay / tremolo / flanger / phaser processing, buried-in-mix vocals, washy droning sustain.

name: San Francisco Bay Area thrash metal studios (Music Annex / Prairie Sun 1983-1991)
note: The San Francisco Bay Area indie-commercial recording studios that tracked the canonical Bay Area thrash metal canon from 1983-1991 — Music Annex Studios Menlo Park (the founding 1983 thrash recording), Prairie Sun Recording Cotati (1986 mixing and tracking landmarks), One on One Recording Sherman Oaks (the 1988 landmark), Sweet Silence Studios Copenhagen (1985 tracking with the canonical thrash producer-engineer).

name: Düsseldorf / Cologne krautrock studios (Kling Klang / Wolperath 1968-1980)
note: The Düsseldorf / Cologne / Wümme indie-commercial recording studios that tracked the canonical German krautrock canon from 1968-1980 — Kling Klang Studio Düsseldorf (the 1974-1977 electronic-pop landmarks), the producer-engineer-owned studio at Wolperath near Cologne (the canonical krautrock engineering room, also hosting late-70s British-German collaborations), Inner Space Studio Weilerswist (the 1971-1973 landmarks).
