name: Twelve-tone equal temperament
sub: 12-TET — the unmarked Western default
note: Octave divided into twelve equal logarithmic steps. Compromises every interval slightly so all keys are equally usable. Locked into standard piano, fixed-fret guitars, valved brass. The recorded-music default, often invisible.

name: Just intonation
sub: pure whole-number frequency ratios
note: Intervals tuned to whole-number ratios — 3:2 fifth, 5:4 third, 9:8 second. Every consonance is beat-free, ringing in sympathy. The catch: you can only stay in one key. Modulating breaks the math.

name: Pythagorean tuning
sub: stacked pure fifths
note: Octave generated by stacking pure 3:2 fifths. Fifths and fourths sing; thirds are sharp and biting. Native to medieval European music, Eastern European folk fiddle, and any tradition where drone and unison matter more than chordal harmony.

name: Meantone temperament
sub: compromised fifths to keep pure thirds
note: Renaissance and early Baroque solution. Fifths are flattened slightly so major thirds can be pure. Consonant in keys close to home, strained in keys far away — which is why those keys carried emotional resonance in period music.

name: Well temperament
sub: unequal temperament where every key works (differently)
note: Late Baroque and early classical. Each key gets its own character — some bright and pure, some darker and more strained. The reason every prelude in The Well-Tempered Clavier sounds different in mood, not just pitch.

name: 19-tone equal temperament
sub: 19-EDO — finer thirds, usable across keys
note: Octave divided into 19 equal steps. Major thirds approach pure 5:4 closely. Some intervals from twelve-tone disappear, others appear. A staple of mid-twentieth-century xenharmonic experiments.

name: 31-tone equal temperament
sub: 31-EDO — extended meantone
note: Approaches quarter-comma meantone but closes the cycle. Used in some twentieth-century European compositions and microtonal jazz. Rich harmonic possibilities beyond the seven-note scale.

name: 24-tone equal temperament (quarter-tones)
sub: 24-EDO — equal-temperament microtonal
note: Twelve-tone with extra notes between every step. The most common entry point for Western composers exploring microtonality, and a rough equivalent for some maqam pitches.

name: Arabic maqam framework
sub: modal system with neutral seconds and thirds
note: Not just a scale — a modal system with characteristic phrases, hierarchical pitches, and ornamentation conventions. Pitches sit between Western steps; neutral seconds and thirds fall halfway. Approximated by 24-EDO, but maqam practitioners often use finer commas.

name: Hindustani shruti system
sub: 22 microtonal divisions per octave
note: A theoretical framework of 22 shruti per octave; in practice, raga performance treats specific shruti as structural and others as inflections. Sympathetic-string instruments make these inflections audible as ringing in the air after the note.

name: Gagaku ryo and ritsu modes
sub: Japanese imperial court modal system
note: Two main modal families — ryo (yang, brighter) and ritsu (yin, more pensive). Tuning differs subtly from Western expectations and varies by ensemble and instrument. The shō's tone clusters expand the harmonic field beyond melody.

name: Mbira seven-tone tuning
sub: ensemble-self-tuned, no fixed reference
note: Each mbira is tuned to itself; two instruments will not share pitch. Heptatonic with intervals that don't map to twelve-tone. The buzz from the machachara and deze adds a halo of difference tones that becomes part of the music.

name: Well temperament — north-German baroque circulating
sub: Werckmeister III: every key works, each colored differently
note: Andreas Werckmeister's 1691 circulating temperament: four specific fifths each tempered by a quarter of the Pythagorean comma, the rest left pure. Every key is playable; each carries its own affective character. The most likely candidate for the temperament Bach had in mind for The Well-Tempered Clavier.

name: Well temperament — late-baroque Italian
sub: Vallotti: six fifths tempered, six pure
note: Francescantonio Vallotti's mid-eighteenth-century Italian circulating temperament: six fifths on the sharp side flattened by a sixth of the syntonic comma each, the other six pure. Milder key-character contrasts than Werckmeister. Standard option for HIP performance of late-baroque Italian repertoire.

name: 22-tone equal temperament
sub: 22-EDO — superpyth fifths, sharp thirds
note: Octave divided into 22 equal steps. Fifths slightly wider than just (closer to 7:5 territory than 3:2), thirds farther from pure 5:4. Native to a body of late-twentieth-century microtonal composition exploring "superpythagorean" harmonic territory and South Asian shruti-grid analysis.

name: 53-tone equal temperament
sub: 53-EDO — Pythagorean-comma grid
note: Octave divided into 53 equal steps, almost identical to a chain of pure Pythagorean fifths. The theoretical basis for Ottoman Turkish makam analysis, where pitches are notated in commas (one-, four-, five-, eight-, nine-comma flats and sharps). Also approximates pure thirds, fifths, and harmonic sevenths within fractions of a cent.

name: 72-tone equal temperament
sub: 72-EDO — twelfth-tone analysis grid
note: Octave divided into 72 equal steps (twelfth-tones). Often used as a precise notational and analytical grid for Carnatic shruti, Byzantine chant inflections, and twentieth-century microtonal jazz. Approximates pure 11-limit ratios within a few cents.

name: Persian dastgah tuning
sub: tetrachord families with koron and sori
note: Twelve modal systems (dastgah-ha) built from tetrachord families with characteristic accidental positions: koron lowering a pitch by roughly a third of a tone, sori raising it by a similar amount. Not 24-EDO quarter-tones; the actual intervals derive from Pythagorean-comma reasoning and vary slightly between dastgah-ha. Each carries its own gushe-ha (melodic kernels) and emotional terrain.

name: Turkish makam (53-comma)
sub: Ottoman-tradition modal system on 53-EDO grid
note: Turkish art-music makam: a modal system using a 53-comma-per-octave grid (one-, four-, five-, eight-, nine-comma flats and sharps). Distinct from Arab maqam and Persian dastgah despite shared lineage. Each makam has characteristic seyir (melodic motion) and tetrachord-pentachord assembly, with pitches between Western steps falling at specific commas.

name: Pelog and slendro (Javanese gamelan)
sub: twin tuning systems of central-Javanese court music
note: Two distinct tuning systems of central-Javanese gamelan: pelog (seven pitches per octave with unequal steps; pathet/mode chooses five) and slendro (five near-equally-spaced pitches per octave). Each gamelan set is tuned to itself — no two gamelans share absolute pitch — and a complete court ensemble has both in matched pelog/slendro pairs.

name: Pelog and slendro (Balinese gamelan)
sub: paired tuning with ombak beating
note: Balinese pelog and slendro share names with the Javanese systems but tune higher and brighter, and pair instruments in umbang/isep — slightly detuned twins whose beating creates the characteristic shimmering ombak ("wave") that defines the Balinese sound. Tunings vary regionally: kebyar, gong gede, semar pegulingan all have distinct intonations.

name: Chinese five-tone (gong/shang/jue/zhi/yu)
sub: pentatonic modal system based on cycle-of-fifths
note: Chinese musical tradition organizes pitch around a five-note pentatonic core (gōng 宮, shāng 商, jué 角, zhǐ 徵, yǔ 羽) generated by cycle-of-fifths progression from a reference pitch. Heptatonic extensions add biàn (变) altered tones for specific repertoire (e.g., yayue court music) but most folk and popular tradition stays pentatonic-rooted. Distinct mode-rotation produces five mode-categories (gong-mode, shang-mode, etc.) characterized by different starting pitch within the same five-tone collection. Used by Chinese, Vietnamese, and broader East-Asian-pentatonic traditions.

name: Thai/Khmer equal heptatonic
sub: seven equal divisions of the octave
note: Thai classical (piphat) and Cambodian classical (pinpeat) instruments are tuned to seven equal divisions of the octave — close to but distinct from Western diatonic. Modes are selected from this 7-tone set rather than added accidentals. Intonation is consistent across xylophone-family instruments (ranat, roneat) and gives this music its characteristic equilibrium between Western and Indonesian-gamelan ear-territory.

name: West African equal heptatonic (Mande balafon)
sub: seven near-equal divisions on the gourd-resonated xylophone
note: Mande-tradition balafon (Mali, Guinea, Senegal, Burkina) is tuned to seven near-equal divisions of the octave, similar in spirit to Thai equal-heptatonic but with regional and maker variation. Susu and Sosso traditions diverge into different scales — pentatonic vs. heptatonic — within the same instrument family. The Sosso bala in Niagassola, Guinea is the historical anchor.

name: Hawaiian slack-key open tunings
sub: kī hōʻalu — open-tuned guitar with sympathetic resonance
note: Family of open guitar tunings developed in Hawaii after Mexican vaqueros introduced the instrument in the nineteenth century. Taro patch (open G), wahine ("woman") tunings (typically open D7), Mauna Loa, double slack — each family lineage often kept its tunings secret, lowering ("slacking") strings to create the warm sympathetic-resonance bath the genre depends on. The song repertoire and the tuning are inseparable.

name: Old-time fiddle cross-tunings
sub: AEAE, ADAE, GDGD scordaturas with sympathetic ringing
note: Appalachian and old-time fiddle traditions retune away from standard GDAE: AEAE ("high bass"), ADAE ("Calico"), GDGD, and many others. Each tuning makes specific keys ring with sympathetic open strings and drones, and locks the player into characteristic tune-families. The Hardanger fiddle in Norway extends the principle further with its sympathetic understrings.

name: Bohlen-Pierce non-octave scale
sub: thirteen equal steps in a tritave (3:1)
note: Discovered independently by Heinz Bohlen, Kees van Prooijen, and John R. Pierce in the 1970s-80s. The octave is replaced by the tritave (3:1 perfect twelfth) divided into 13 equal steps. Eliminates the 2:1 octave entirely. The scale highlights odd-harmonic (3, 5, 7, 9, 11) consonance and produces music that sounds tonally coherent yet utterly unfamiliar.

name: Extended just intonation (43-tone)
sub: twentieth-century American 11-limit just intonation
note: A 43-tone "monophonic just intonation" — pitches built from prime ratios up to and including 11, organized as a tonality diamond around a 1/1 fundamental. Designed to allow modulation between just-tuned chords. Required custom-built instruments (chromelodeon, kithara, harmonic canons) since no standard instrument can play it. The American root of an entire twentieth-century JI tradition.

name: Tuareg pentatonic with raised 4th
sub: 1-2-3-#4-5-6 hexatonic with desert-blues surface
note: The defining modal vocabulary of Tuareg desert blues, derived from imzad (single-string bowed fiddle) and tehardent (three-string lute) repertoire. Pentatonic 1-2-3-5-6 with a frequent raised 4th producing the "blues" surface that misleads Western listeners into hearing Mississippi delta — but the genealogy is Saharan modal, not Atlantic. Tunes are short cyclic forms with a 4- to 12-bar harmonic cycle, often a single chord with passing IV or ♭VII. Capos at 2nd, 3rd, 5th, 7th frets are common; absolute keys cluster in E, A, D, F#m, Bm.

name: Kignit Tezeta (major variant)
sub: Ethiopian pentatonic — mode of nostalgia/longing
note: C–D–E–G–A (1–2–3–5–6), the major-pentatonic Tezeta — the mode of nostalgia, longing, memory in Ethiopian musical tradition. Authentic tuning is not equal-tempered: krar and masenqo are tuned by ear in pure temperament, so the intervals are subtly stretched/compressed relative to 12-TET. The Ethio-jazz Golden Age canon sits heavily in this mode.

name: Kignit Tezeta (minor variant)
sub: Ethiopian pentatonic — minor mode of longing
note: C–E♭–F–G–B♭ (1–♭3–4–5–♭7), the minor-pentatonic Tezeta variant. Slightly more melancholy than the major Tezeta. Common in Ethio-jazz ballads. Pure temperament authentic; equal-tempered approximation acceptable for fusion contexts.

name: Kignit Bati (major variant)
sub: Ethiopian pentatonic — mode of laments
note: Major Bati pentatonic — closely related to minor Tezeta in some analyses, distinct in others. Mode of laments and elegies in Ethiopian tradition.

name: Kignit Bati (minor variant)
sub: Ethiopian pentatonic — heavy lament mode
note: C–D♭–F–G–A♭ (1–♭2–4–5–♭6), the minor-pentatonic Bati. Phrygian-tinged with characteristic ♭2 and ♭6. The mode of deepest lament. Heard in slow Ethio-jazz ballads and in azmari elegies.

name: Kignit Ambassel
sub: Ethiopian pentatonic — mode of historical/heroic songs
note: C–D♭–F–G♭–A (1–♭2–4–♭5–6) in one common analysis; Mixolydian-pentatonic variant C–D–F–G–A also documented. Mode of historical/heroic narrative songs in Amhara tradition. The defining mode of Wollo (Ambassel region) folk repertoire from which the name comes.

name: Kignit Anchihoye
sub: Ethiopian pentatonic — slow-danceable mode
note: C–D♭–F–G♭–A in one analysis. Same intervals as one Ambassel variant in some sources but with distinct rhythmic conventions — slower yet still danceable. Common in azmari and Eskista repertoire.

name: Sintir three-string D-D-G (or C-C-F)
sub: Gnawa bass-lute drone+octave+fourth tuning
note: The sintir/guembri/hajhouj is tuned in three strings: lowest string is a drone; middle string (thinnest) tuned an octave above the drone and never fretted; third string tuned a fourth above the drone. D-D-G is the most-cited modern reference tuning (low D drone, high D octave, G fourth); C-C-F and other keys appear depending on the zaouia tradition and the maâlem's vocal range. The middle string being thinner and an octave higher is the defining acoustic feature.

name: Samba 2/4 with telecoteco / partido-alto feel
sub: Brazilian samba rhythmic foundation in two
note: Samba is fundamentally in 2/4 (not 4/4 — the bar lines are half the length a non-Brazilian ear assumes). Surdo de primeira on beat 2, surdo de segunda on beat 1, tamborim with the telecoteco syncopated 16th-note pattern, pandeiro with thumb-fingertip-palm-fingertip 4-stroke. Partido-alto is a subfeel within samba with strong upbeat emphasis and longer-form responsorial vocals.

name: Choro 2/4 with characteristic syncopation
sub: Brazilian choro melodic-rhythmic feel
note: Choro in 2/4 with the characteristic syncopation derived from polka, schottische, and habanera fused with African-Brazilian rhythmic accents. Bandolim or flute carries the melody; violão de 7 cordas plays the bordão countermelody walking-bass; pandeiro and sometimes cavaquinho provide rhythm. Tempos typically 100–160 BPM. The form predates samba.

name: Baião 2/4 with zabumba-on-beat-1 bass
sub: Northeast Brazilian baião / forró feel
note: Baião is in 2/4 with the zabumba bass-drum stick stroke on beat 1 (the "dum" of the dum-tum-tchi pattern), with the bacalhau high stroke on the "and" of beat 1 and triângulo providing the open-closed pattern. Accordion (sanfona) carries the melody. Forró extends the same rhythmic foundation to dance-band format.

name: Frevo 2/4 fast carnival-march feel
sub: Pernambuco carnival brass-band frenetic 2/4
note: Frevo in 2/4 at 110–160 BPM with brass-band foreground (multiple trumpets, trombones, saxophones, tuba), military-snare and brake-drum percussion, and the characteristic frevo march-derived rhythmic feel that supports the passo dance with its sombrinha (small umbrella). Two main subforms: frevo de rua (instrumental street frevo) and frevo-canção (with vocals). Distinct from samba 2/4 by faster tempo, march-band instrumentation, and absence of surdo-based foundation.

name: Maracatu nação 4/4 with alfaia foundation
sub: Pernambuco carnival cortejo procession feel
note: Maracatu nação (cortejo / de baque virado) in 4/4 with alfaia bass drums providing the foundational pattern, gonguê bell laying the time, caixa snare and mineiro shaker filling the texture, and agbê (gourd-and-bead) shakers. The procession context (cortejo) shapes tempo (slow processional 70–95 BPM) and song-form (responsorial chorus on toada melodies). Distinct from maracatu rural / cabocolinho.

name: Capoeira berimbau toques (rhythmic modal patterns)
sub: Bahian capoeira berimbau toque vocabulary
note: Capoeira is led by the berimbau with specific toques (rhythmic patterns) that signal the type of jogo (game). Angola (slow, sneaky 60–90 BPM), São Bento Grande de Angola (medium 90–110), São Bento Grande de Regional (fast 110–140), Iuna (slow ritual, masters-only), Cavalaria (signaling warning historically of approaching police). Three berimbau pitches (gunga lowest, médio, viola highest) interlock in polyrhythmic counterpoint. Atabaque marks the time; pandeiro fills.

name: Gamelan slendro (5-tone, near-equidistant)
sub: Javanese / Balinese gamelan 5-tone tuning system
note: Slendro is one of the two principal tuning systems of Indonesian gamelan. Five pitches per octave at approximately equidistant intervals (≈240 cents each, slightly varied by ensemble — every gamelan set is uniquely tuned). NOT equivalent to Western pentatonic. Used for serene, contemplative repertoire in Javanese tradition; for many gong kebyar pieces in Balinese tradition. The Western 12-TET approximation distorts the mode fundamentally.

name: Gamelan pelog (7-tone, unequal)
sub: Javanese / Balinese gamelan 7-tone tuning system with characteristic semitone-and-large-step pattern
note: Pelog is the other principal gamelan tuning. Seven pitches per octave with characteristic unequal spacing — mix of narrow semitone-like intervals and wider whole-tone-and-larger steps. Used for solemn, ceremonial repertoire in Javanese tradition; for many religious pieces in Balinese tradition. Common pathets (modal subsets): pelog bem, pelog barang, pelog nem. Each ensemble has its own unique pelog tuning.

name: Japanese in scale (semitone-containing, sad)
sub: Japanese pentatonic with semitone, somber affect
note: The in scale (陰旋法) is the principal "minor-key" Japanese pentatonic: 1-♭2-4-5-♭6 (e.g., D-E♭-G-A-B♭). Used in shakuhachi honkyoku, koto Yatsuhashi-school repertoire, shamisen min-yō folk songs, and most somber traditional Japanese repertoire. Distinct from Western minor pentatonic by the characteristic ♭2 (the "Japanese half-step" interval).

name: Japanese yo scale (no semitones, bright)
sub: Japanese pentatonic without semitones, cheerful affect
note: The yo scale (陽旋法) is the principal "major-key" Japanese pentatonic: 1-2-4-5-6 (e.g., D-E-G-A-B). Used in upbeat min-yō folk songs, gagaku ryo-mode repertoire, festival music. No semitones — the "bright" Japanese mode. Distinct from Western major pentatonic by the differing harmonic context.

name: Chinese pentatonic (wuyin scale)
sub: Chinese five-tone scale with gong / shang / jiao / zhi / yu modes
note: The Chinese pentatonic (五音 wuyin) is the foundational scale of Chinese traditional music: gong (1) — shang (2) — jiao (3) — zhi (5) — yu (6). Five modes by rotation: gong-mode (major-like), shang-mode (Dorian-like), jiao-mode (Phrygian-pentatonic), zhi-mode (Mixolydian-like), yu-mode (minor-like). Underlies guqin solo, yueju opera melodies, jiangnan sizhu chamber music, and most Han Chinese folk repertoire. Pure-pentatonic; semitones added as biàn-yǔ and biàn-gōng decorative tones rarely.

name: Korean jeongak modes (gye-myeon-jo / pyeong-jo)
sub: Korean court-music modal system
note: Jeongak (정악, court music) uses two principal modes: pyeong-jo (평조, "level mode" — major-pentatonic-like) and gye-myeon-jo (계면조, "boundary mode" — minor-pentatonic-with-microtonal-bends). Each mode is realized with characteristic ornamentation (sigimsae), pitch bends, and characteristic note functions. Tempo is generally slow, sustained, with deep breath-pulse rhythm. Distinct from minsogak folk modes.

name: Korean minsogak modes (sanjo / pansori scales)
sub: Korean folk-music modal system with regional dialects
note: Minsogak (민속악, folk music) uses regional modal dialects: gyeong-toritori (Seoul/Gyeonggi), menari-tori (East/Gangwon), yukjabaegi-tori (Southwest/Jeolla — used in pansori), susimga-tori (Northwest). Each tori has characteristic scalar shape, ornamentation, breath-pulse, and pitch-bend vocabulary. The yukjabaegi-tori with its descending-fourth tonic and heavy sigimsae bending is the signature mode of pansori.

name: Mongolian / Tuvan khoomei harmonic-overtone vocabulary
sub: Throat-singing harmonic-series modal system
note: Khoomei (Tuvan) / khoomii (Mongolian) overtone singing operates on the harmonic series of a sustained vocal-cord fundamental, with the singer selectively amplifying upper partials (4th through 12th harmonics typically) through tongue-and-mouth resonance to produce a separate audible melody above the drone. Five principal styles: khoomei (medium-range), sygyt (high whistle), kargyraa (low growl), borbangnadyr, ezengileer. The harmonic-series tuning is intrinsically just/pure — Western 12-TET notation only approximates it.

name: Tibetan Gyuto / Gyume multiphonic chant
sub: Tibetan Buddhist tantric chant with vocal multiphonics
note: Gyuto and Gyume Tantric colleges train monks in dzo-ke (deep-rumble) and gyer-skad (intoned-recitation) chant styles that produce audible multiphonics — a fundamental near 70-90 Hz with the 5th and 10th harmonics simultaneously audible as the perceived melody. The intoned-recitation register sits roughly a third lower than ordinary speech, supported by diaphragmatic breath. Tuning is intrinsically harmonic-series. Used for sadhana (visualization-practice) liturgy and especially for the protector deity Vajrabhairava cycle.

name: Thai seven-equal tuning (saep song chan)
sub: Thai classical 7-equidistant-intervals tuning
note: Thai classical music uses a 7-tone-equal-tempered scale (≈171.4 cents per step) — NOT the Western diatonic. Every interval is the same size; there are no semitones or whole tones in the Western sense. The piphat ensemble (ranat ek, ranat thum, khong wong yai, khong wong lek, pi nai, taphon, klong khaek, ching, chap) and mahori chamber ensemble are tuned to this system. Western 12-TET notation grossly misrepresents the pitch system.

name: Son clave 3-2 forward
sub: Cuban son clave in 3-side-first orientation
note: The 3-side-first orientation of son clave: beats fall on 1, 2.5, 4 of bar one (the 3-side, three strikes), then 2, 3 of bar two (the 2-side, two strikes). This is the rhythmic spine of son cubano, son montuno, mambo, and the entire son family. Every melodic and harmonic event in son-family music is positioned relative to the clave — "playing in clave" vs "crossed clave" is the defining grammatical question. Distinct from rumba clave (which has the 4-side strike delayed by an eighth-note).

name: Son clave 2-3 reverse
sub: Cuban son clave in 2-side-first orientation (common in salsa)
note: The 2-side-first orientation: bar one has the 2-side (beats 2 and 3), bar two has the 3-side. Less common in traditional Cuban son but very common in Fania-era NY salsa (the song-form structure often opens with a 2-side phrase). Same rhythmic content as 3-2, just rotated by a bar.

name: Rumba clave 3-2 (delayed 4-side strike)
sub: Afro-Cuban rumba clave, distinct from son clave
note: Rumba clave differs from son clave in the position of the third strike on the 3-side: son clave hits on the "and" of beat 2 (eighth-note before beat 3); rumba clave hits on beat 3 (a quarter-note later). This delayed strike is the defining rhythmic difference and gives rumba its more syncopated, less square feel. Used in yambú, guaguancó, columbia, and the broader Afro-Cuban folkloric tradition. Distinct from son clave.

name: Tango 4/4 with marcato compás
sub: Argentine tango rhythmic foundation in 4/4 with characteristic marcato bass accents
note: Tango is in 4/4 (NOT 2/4 as sometimes notated for visual brevity) with marcato compás — the bass and piano left hand mark beats 1 and 3 strongly, with bandoneon syncopations layered against this anchor. Tango forms (canción, milonga-tango, instrumental tango) all share this 4/4 marcato foundation but vary in tempo (slow tango canción 60-80 BPM, fast tango 100-130). The orquesta típica articulates the compás through the rhythm section (piano-bass-sometimes-drums) while the bandoneon-violin frontline carries the melody.

name: Milonga 2/4 with ostinato bass
sub: Argentine milonga, faster than tango, with characteristic ostinato
note: Milonga in 2/4 at 100-150 BPM (faster than tango), with the characteristic habanera-derived ostinato bass: dotted-eighth + sixteenth + quarter + quarter. The form predates tango and shares ancestry with the Cuban habanera. Two principal subforms: milonga campera (rural, slower, song-form) and milonga ciudadana (urban, faster, dance-form).

name: Cumbia 4/4 paseo feel
sub: Colombian cumbia rhythmic foundation in 4/4 with dotted-eighth syncopation
note: Cumbia in 4/4 at 80-115 BPM with the characteristic dotted-eighth + sixteenth + quarter pattern in the tambora (bass drum). The llamador (smaller drum) marks the off-beat. The gaita flutes or accordion carry the melody. Mexican cumbia, Peruvian chicha, and Argentine cumbia villera all derive from the Colombian original but with regional rhythm-section substitutions.

name: Vallenato four airs (paseo, son, merengue, puya)
sub: Colombian vallenato rhythmic vocabulary across four air types
note: Vallenato has four canonical airs: paseo (slowest, lyrical, song-form), son (medium, narrative), merengue (fast, not the Dominican merengue), and puya (fastest, virtuosic accordion showpiece). The caja (drum) pattern shifts between airs; the guacharaca scraper marks the time. The Hohner three-row button accordion (often a Corona III) is the canonical lead instrument. Festival Vallenato (Valledupar, annual) judges competitions in each of the four airs separately.

name: Mariachi son jalisciense 6/8 + 3/4 hemiola
sub: Mariachi son polymeter with simultaneous 6/8 and 3/4 feels
note: The mariachi son jalisciense (and the broader Mexican son family from which it derives) uses sesquialtera — the simultaneous and audible polymetric layering of 6/8 (two groups of three eighths) and 3/4 (three groups of two eighths) within the same bar. The guitarrón typically marks the 3/4 strong beats with octave-pair plucks; the violins and trumpets sing across in 6/8. Listener perception flips between the two feels. Distinct from straight 6/8 or straight 3/4.

name: Ranchera 3/4 vals and 2/4 polka subforms
sub: Mexican ranchera rhythmic vocabulary across waltz and polka-derived subforms
note: Ranchera has two principal rhythmic subforms: ranchera de vals (3/4 waltz, slow-medium tempo, sentimental song-form) and ranchera de polka (2/4 polka-derived, faster, dance-friendly). Sometimes ranchera lenta (slow 4/4 ballad) is recognized as a third. The golden-age canon spans all three. Distinct from corrido (narrative ballad, also typically 3/4 or 4/4) which is a separate Mexican song-form.

name: Merengue 2/4 perico ripiao
sub: Dominican merengue rhythmic foundation, fast 2/4 with tambora foundation
note: Merengue dominicano in 2/4 at 130-180 BPM. The tambora (double-headed barrel drum) plays the foundational hand-and-stick pattern; the güira (metal scraper) plays the constant sixteenth-note pattern; the accordion or saxophones carry the melody. Two main subforms: merengue típico / perico ripiao (small-group rural, accordion-led) and merengue de orquesta (big-band, saxophone-led).

name: Bachata 4/4 with bongo pickup
sub: Dominican bachata rhythmic foundation, 4/4 with bongo syncopation and characteristic bongo pickup at end of bar
note: Bachata in 4/4 at 100-130 BPM. Two electric guitars (lead — requinto-style, and rhythm — segunda), an electric bass, bongos, and güira. The bongo plays a characteristic pickup figure at the end of each four-bar phrase (bongo "rolls" or "picao"), which is the defining grammatical event of bachata rhythm-section playing. Lead guitar is melismatic, ornamented, with bent notes and slides drawn from bolero romántico and son cubano.

name: Huayno 2/4 Andean pentatonic dance
sub: Quechua/Aymara Andean dance-song in 2/4 with anhemitonic pentatonic mode
note: Huayno in 2/4 at 90-140 BPM, in anhemitonic pentatonic mode (no semitones — 1, 2, ♭3, 5, ♭7 in approximate Western terms, though tunings vary by community). The dance pattern is short-short-long. Charango (small armadillo-back lute) carries the melody; quena (notched flute) and zampoña (panpipe set) double the line; bombo andino marks the bass pulse. Distinct from sikuri (panpipe ensemble in 2/4 ostinato pattern) and from cueca (3/4 hemiola dance further south).

name: Joropo 3/4 corrido with hemiola
sub: Venezuelan-Colombian llanos plains 3/4 with frequent hemiola
note: Joropo in 3/4 (or 6/8, the two notations are alternative renderings of the same feel) with frequent hemiola shifts. Multiple subforms: joropo recio (fast virtuosic), pasaje (slower lyrical), zumba que zumba, golpe. The arpa llanera (32-string diatonic harp) carries the melody with virtuosic right-hand runs; the cuatro venezolano (4-string strummed lute) provides harmony-and-rhythm; the maracas mark the pulse. The vocal style — verso llanero — is declamatory, narrative, with characteristic alaridos (sustained cries).

name: Jazz swing-eighth 4/4
sub: American jazz swing-feel eighth-note subdivision in 4/4
note: The defining rhythmic feel of American jazz from swing through bebop, hard bop, modal, and post-bop. Eighth notes are NOT played evenly — the on-beat eighth is held longer than the off-beat (roughly a 2:1 triplet-derived ratio at medium tempos, evening out toward 1:1 at fast tempos). The ride cymbal articulates the canonical "spang-a-lang" pattern (quarter, eighth-eighth swung); the walking bass marks four-on-the-floor quarters; the snare and hi-hat fill in syncopated comping figures. Distinct from straight (even) eighths of Latin jazz or fusion.

name: Bebop complex chord-change vocabulary
sub: Bebop harmonic vocabulary built on chord-substitution and tritone substitution
note: Bebop harmonic practice from Parker, Gillespie, Powell, Monk onward — built on rapid chord-changes (often two chords per bar in II-V-I cascades), tritone substitution (replacing dominant chords with the dominant a tritone away), altered dominants (♭9, ♯9, ♭13, ♯11), and extended chord voicings reaching to thirteenths. The improvising line traces these harmonic events with chromatic approach-tones, enclosure patterns, and patterned melodic cells. Distinct from modal jazz (which holds one chord/mode for many bars) and from free jazz (which dispenses with chord-changes entirely).

name: Modal jazz Dorian-and-other static-mode framework
sub: Modal jazz harmonic practice — one mode held for many bars
note: Modal jazz harmonic practice from the late-1950s and post-1960 modal canon. The form holds one mode (often Dorian, sometimes Aeolian or Mixolydian) for eight or sixteen bars at a time, dispensing with the rapid bebop chord-cascade. The bassist plays modal-tone-anchored rather than chord-root-walking lines. The improvising line explores the mode rather than tracking changes. The harmonic mood is open, suspended, less directional than bebop.

name: Free jazz no-changes framework
sub: Free jazz dispensing with fixed harmonic structure
note: Free jazz from 1960 onward — dispensing with fixed chord progressions and often with steady meter as well. Players operate in "pitch areas" rather than chord-and-mode, in textural energy-bursts rather than melodic-line. Collective improvisation rather than soloist-and-rhythm-section. Often extreme dynamics (very loud, very soft), extended techniques (multiphonics, altissimo, growling, percussive valve effects), and durations that depart from standard song-form lengths.

name: Latin jazz clave-overlay framework
sub: Latin jazz harmonic-and-rhythmic vocabulary combining jazz changes with Afro-Cuban clave
note: Latin jazz vocabulary from the 1940s (Cubop) through the modern canon — combining jazz chord-changes (bebop II-V-I cascades, modal voicings) with the rhythmic spine of son or rumba clave. The piano plays montuno (cyclic Cuban accompaniment patterns) on the changes; the rhythm section is congas, bongos, timbales, claves, often with a jazz drum kit added. Bass line shifts to a tumbao (Cuban anticipating-bass pattern) rather than a walking-bass.

name: Folk fingerstyle alternating-bass (Travis picking)
sub: Alternating-bass right-hand fingerstyle pattern used in American folk
note: The defining right-hand pattern of 20th-century American folk and country fingerstyle: thumb alternates between root and fifth on the bass strings while the index, middle, and ring fingers play melody or arpeggios on the higher strings, creating an audible pulse-plus-melody texture from a single instrument. Codified in 1940s-50s Kentucky country playing, then absorbed into the Greenwich Village folk revival and the laurel canyon singer-songwriter vocabulary.

name: Open-tuning singer-songwriter vocabulary (DADGAD, CGDGCD, open D, open G)
sub: Non-standard guitar tunings characteristic of 70s singer-songwriter and folk
note: Non-standard guitar tunings (i.e., not E-A-D-G-B-E) characteristic of the 70s Laurel Canyon and Greenwich Village singer-songwriter aesthetic and the British/Celtic folk revival. Some singer-songwriters used dozens of distinct tunings (CGDFCE, DADF#AD, DADGBE, etc.) to access modal voicings and bell-like sustained intervals not available in standard tuning. DADGAD (D-A-D-G-A-D) is the canonical Celtic folk tuning. Open G (D-G-D-G-B-D) is the blues slide vocabulary. Each tuning forces the player out of standard chord shapes and into characteristic voicings with sustained ringing strings.

name: Americana train-beat 4/4
sub: Americana / honky-tonk train-beat rhythmic pattern in 4/4
note: The defining rhythmic pattern of mid-century country and the contemporary Americana / alt-country canon — a 4/4 train-beat in which the snare drum plays a constant eighth-note pattern (boom-tick-boom-tick) evocative of locomotive wheels, with the kick on beats 1 and 3 and the snare backbeat on 2 and 4. The walking bass line moves quarter-note-per-beat. Tempo typically 90-130 BPM. Distinct from the boom-chuck honky-tonk 2/4 (lighter, faster) and from the country shuffle (triplet feel).

name: American primitive open-tuning drone-raga framework
sub: Open-tuning fingerstyle drone-and-raga vocabulary of the John Fahey lineage
note: The defining harmonic-and-rhythmic framework of American primitive guitar from Fahey Blind Joe Death (1959) onward: open-tuning steel-string acoustic in DADGAD, open C (CGCGCE), drop D, or custom-derived tunings; right-hand alternating-bass-plus-melody Travis-derived fingerpicking with the thumb often laying down a sustained drone pedal; harmonic vocabulary fusing Mississippi Delta-blues vamps, ragtime cadential figures, Appalachian hymnody, Indian raga modal-suspension (especially in Basho_s 12-string raga adaptations), and 20th-century minimalist-classical ostinato. Forms vary from short blues-frame pieces (Fahey early) through long-form raga arcs (Basho Visions of the Country, 30 Days) to virtuosic melody-foregrounded showpieces (Kottke 6 and 12 String Guitar). Distinct from folk-revival singer-songwriter open-tunings (which are voice-accompaniment) and from contemporary acoustic fingerstyle (Tommy Emmanuel et al., which is technique-foregrounded entertainment).

name: Gothic Americana minor-modal Old-Testament vocabulary
sub: Minor-key modal harmonic vocabulary for Southern Gothic Americana lyrical content
note: The harmonic-and-thematic framework characteristic of Gothic Americana — the Southern Gothic literary tradition (Faulkner, Flannery OConnor, Cormac McCarthy) translated into folk-country instrumentation. Minor-key default tonal center (most often A minor, D minor, or E minor), Aeolian-mode default with frequent Dorian and Phrygian touches for biblical-ancient atmosphere. Vocal delivery is declamatory, Pentecostal-derived (Sixteen Horsepower_s David Eugene Edwards came from a Nazarene/Pentecostal upbringing) or Baptist-revival (Reverend Glasseye, Slim Cessna). Banjo, fiddle, accordion, and distorted hurdy-gurdy carry harmonic-melodic load with strong drone pedals. Themes: death, divine judgment, sin, the Old Testament, frontier violence, the South_s buried histories. Distinct from gothic_country (which is the same family but narrower) and from folk_noir (which has Victorian / chamber / European-literary roots rather than Southern Gothic / Pentecostal roots).

name: Folk noir Aeolian-Phrygian chamber-folk framework
sub: Dark chamber-folk modal vocabulary in the Marissa Nadler / Espers tradition
note: The harmonic-atmospheric framework of contemporary folk noir — the broader Kemado / Mexican Summer / Hexham Head circle. Minor-key default, Aeolian and Phrygian modal centers with frequent suspended fourths and sustained-resolution voicings; fingerpicked acoustic guitar foregrounding fingernail-on-string brightness; chamber instrumentation (cello, viola, harmonium, piano, occasional sparse percussion); voice tracked with characteristic long-tail reverb that places the vocal in a "haunted-room" atmosphere distinct from singer-songwriter dry-vocal. Lyrical content draws from Victorian / pre-Raphaelite imagery, gothic-novel atmosphere, surrealist poetry, cinematic-noir reference. Distinct from gothic_americana (Southern Gothic / Pentecostal lineage) and from neofolk-apocalyptic (British post-industrial lineage, which uses synth pads and martial percussion alongside acoustic). The original "folk noir" term was coined within the British neofolk scene to distance from the neofolk umbrella, but contemporary usage has broadened to encompass the chamber-folk songwriter tradition.

name: R&B shuffle 12/8 swing-feel blues-ballad framework
sub: Pre-rock-era R&B 12/8 triplet ballad foundation
note: The defining rhythmic framework of late-1940s through 1950s American R&B ballads and slow numbers — 12/8 meter (four groups of three eighth-notes per bar) creating an audible triplet undercurrent against the 4/4 beat. The piano left hand and bass typically walk in quarter notes; the piano right hand or guitar plays triplet-figure chord-comping; the drum kit accents 2 and 4 on the snare with a triplet-shuffle ride pattern. Tempo typically 40-75 BPM. The defining vocabulary of the broader jump-blues-to-classic-R&B transition. Distinct from the straight-eighth boogie shuffle (1940s jump blues) and from the slower-tempo doo-wop 6/8 / 12/8 ballad (which uses similar meter at slower tempo with vocal-group foreground).

name: Motown four-on-floor with tambourine on 2 and 4
sub: Motown-era Northern soul rhythmic foundation
note: The defining Motown rhythmic foundation, codified at Hitsville USA Detroit 1959-1972 by the Funk Brothers rhythm section. Four-on-the-floor kick drum on every quarter; backbeat snare on 2 and 4 reinforced by Jack Ashfords tambourine on the exact same beats (the doubled tambourine + snare backbeat is the defining auditory signature); James Jamersons electric bass plays anticipated-and-syncopated melodic figures that create rhythmic tension against the four-on-floor kick; Earl Van Dykes piano comps on syncopated upbeats; Robert White and Joe Messina guitars play tight chordal stabs or single-note counterpoint. Tempo typically 95-130 BPM. The Northern Soul UK scene later isolated this rhythmic vocabulary as the defining "stomper" feel for the British dance-club circuit. Distinct from Stax / Southern soul (which is more relaxed, less four-on-the-floor) and from Philly soul (which adds strings and 6-piece-or-larger rhythm section).

name: Funk one-and-the-three syncopated 4/4
sub: James Brown / Sly Stone / Parliament-Funkadelic rhythmic vocabulary
note: The defining rhythmic vocabulary of funk from 1965 onward. Defined by the radical recentering of accent onto beat 1 ("on the one") with syncopated sixteenth-note subdivision around that anchor. The drum kit plays a tight 4/4 with the snare often delayed or syncopated against the conventional 2-and-4 backbeat; the electric bass plays popping-and-slapping syncopated figures; the horn section plays staccato chordal stabs on offbeats; the guitar plays muted-strum sixteenth-note chicken-scratch on a single chord (the canonical funk rhythm-guitar technique). Harmonic content is reduced — often one or two chords across an entire song, with the focus on rhythmic interlock rather than chord-change. Tempo typically 95-115 BPM. Distinct from Motown (which is melody-and-pop-arrangement foregrounded) and from soul (which is vocal-and-emotion foregrounded).

name: Doo-wop changes 1950s I-vi-IV-V progression
sub: 1950s doo-wop harmonic-and-rhythmic ballad framework
note: The defining harmonic-rhythmic framework of 1950s American doo-wop — the I-vi-IV-V chord progression (in C major: C-Am-F-G) repeated cyclically as a vocal-group accompaniment frame. Often in 12/8 ballad meter at 60-90 BPM, with the lead tenor carrying the melody, the bass singer holding the chord root on each change, the baritone holding the third, and the falsetto first tenor singing the "shooby-doo-wop" non-lexical syllabic countermelody that gave the genre its name.

name: Flamenco compás 12-beat cycles (soleá, bulería, alegrías, seguiriya)
sub: Flamenco 12-beat compás cyclic rhythm vocabulary
note: The defining rhythmic framework of flamenco — the 12-beat compás cycle subdivided into accented and unaccented beats varying by palo (flamenco song-form). Soleá: beats 3, 6, 8, 10, 12 accented. Bulería: same 12-beat cycle but at much faster tempo with cross-rhythmic 6+6 acceleration. Alegrías: shares soleá structure but in major-key mood. Seguiriya: 12-beat cycle in 2/4 + 3/4 + 3/4 + 2/4 + 2/4 hemiola pattern, slow-and-tragic mood. Tangos and rumba flamenca use 4/4 instead of 12. Counted by palmas (clappers) and footwork (zapateado) and reflected in the cantaors phrase-endings. Harmonic frame typically uses the Andalusian Phrygian dominant mode (E Phrygian with raised third — E F G# A B C D — equivalent to the Arab/North African maqam Hijaz transposed).

name: Byzantine oktoechos eight-mode system
sub: Byzantine Orthodox liturgical 8-mode modal system
note: The eight-mode (oktoechos) modal system governing Byzantine Orthodox liturgical chant — four authentic modes (protos, devteros, tritos, tetartos) and four plagal modes (their lower-fourth-transposed counterparts: plagios protos, plagios devteros, varys, plagios tetartos). Each mode rotates through the liturgical year on an eight-week cycle. The modal intervals are NOT 12-tone-equal-tempered — Byzantine practice uses moria (subdivisions of the octave into 72 parts) creating microtonal pitch positions that the chanter (psaltis) traces against a drone (ison) sustained by a small chorus. The melismatic chanter performs the melody with characteristic ornamental gestures (apostrophos, klasma, varia) notated in the Byzantine neumatic script. Distinct from the four-mode Gregorian system of Western Christianity and from the makam system of Arab and Turkish music (though Byzantine and Ottoman makam shared significant cross-influence through the Byzantine Empires Ottoman successor period).

name: Celtic Irish modal vocabulary (Dorian and Mixolydian dominant)
sub: Irish trad modal harmonic vocabulary
note: The defining modal vocabulary of Irish trad and the broader Celtic music family (Irish, Scottish, Cape Breton, Welsh, Breton, Asturian, Galician). Most tunes are in Dorian (D Dorian: D E F G A B C D — minor with raised sixth) or Mixolydian (D Mixolydian: D E F# G A B C D — major with lowered seventh), not Western major-or-minor. The modal intervals create the characteristic harmonic ambiguity that distinguishes Celtic music from English-language Anglo-American folk (which is more major-key). The harmonic frame is typically a single drone fifth (D-A on most fiddle and flute tunes), with chord changes occurring rarely and often only at the modal-pivot points. Standard time signatures: jigs in 6/8, reels in 4/4, slip-jigs in 9/8, hornpipes in 4/4 with dotted-eighth feel, polkas in 2/4, marches in 4/4. Tempo varies widely: slow airs at 30-50 BPM, reels at 110-130 BPM, jigs at 90-120 BPM.

name: Rebetiko Eastern modal dromos system
sub: Greek rebetiko makam-derived modal vocabulary (dromoi)
note: The dromos (literally "road" or "path", plural dromoi) modal system of Greek rebetiko — a Greek adaptation of the Ottoman / Arab maqam system brought to Athens and Piraeus by the 1922 Asia Minor refugees from Smyrna, Constantinople, and the broader Anatolian Greek diaspora. Principal dromoi include Rast (similar to Western major with characteristic raised fourth degree), Houseyni (mournful minor with neutral seventh), Saba (Phrygian-dominant tetrachord), Hicaz (Phrygian-dominant), Niavent, Sabach. Each dromos governs not only the modal intervals but also the characteristic melodic phrases (taksim improvisation patterns) and the emotional register of the song.

name: Nordic folk modal drone-and-double-stops vocabulary
sub: Hardanger fiddle / nyckelharpa / kantele modal drone-foundation vocabulary
note: The defining modal-and-textural framework of Nordic folk music — the Hardanger fele (Norwegian Hardanger fiddle), nyckelharpa (Swedish keyed fiddle), and kantele (Finnish lap-zither) all build on sympathetic-string-resonance drone foundations underneath modal melodies. The Hardanger fiddles four-or-five sympathetic strings (resonating below the fingerboard) ring continuously throughout each tune; the nyckelharpas twelve sympathetic strings function similarly; the kantele has open strings tuned to a chord that drone underneath plucked melody. Modal vocabulary leans Mixolydian (raised seventh) and Lydian (raised fourth) more than Dorian. Double-stops on the fiddle are nearly continuous rather than occasional, with the bowed-and-droning open string functioning as a parallel-fifth pedal. Distinct from Irish trad (which has less sympathetic-resonance and is more single-line) and from Eastern European folk fiddle (which uses different ornamental vocabulary).

name: Balkan odd-meter aksak vocabulary (7/8, 9/8, 11/8, 13/8)
sub: Balkan and Bulgarian additive odd-meter rhythmic system
note: The aksak (Turkish for "limping") additive rhythmic system characteristic of Balkan village dance — Bulgarian, Macedonian, Serbian, Greek (northern), Albanian, Romanian traditions. Rather than the symmetric 2-2-2-2 (4/4) or 3-3-3-3 (12/8) Western patterns, aksak groups eighth-notes into asymmetric clusters. Canonical examples: Rachenitsa 7/8 grouped 2+2+3 (Bulgarian); Paidushko 5/8 grouped 2+3; Kopanitsa 11/8 grouped 2+2+3+2+2 (Bulgarian Shopluk region); Lesnoto 7/8 grouped 3+2+2 (Macedonian); Devetorka 9/8 grouped 2+2+2+3 (Bulgarian / Macedonian); Sedmorka 7/16 (Bulgarian fast tempo); Kalamatianos 7/8 grouped 3+2+2 (Greek). The asymmetry is performed-and-felt rather than counted — the characteristic "limping" feel of the 3-step grouping against the 2-step groupings creates the genres signature dance momentum.

name: Klezmer freygish / ahava raba modal vocabulary
sub: Eastern European Ashkenazi Jewish klezmer mode system
note: The modal vocabulary of klezmer (and the parallel synagogue-cantorial khazonus tradition) — a four-mode system shared with the broader Eastern European Ashkenazi Jewish liturgical-and-secular musical tradition. Principal modes: Freygish (also called Ahava Raba, "great love" in Hebrew) — Phrygian dominant scale with characteristic augmented-second between scale degrees 2 and 3, the most distinctively Jewish-sounding mode; Mi Sheberach (also called Ukrainian Dorian) — Dorian with raised fourth, very common in klezmer dance tunes; Magen Avot — Aeolian / natural minor, used for slower mournful or contemplative tunes; Adonai Malach — Mixolydian with characteristic lowered second, less common in secular klezmer but central to the cantorial liturgical setting. The augmented-second interval characteristic of Freygish and Mi Sheberach is the auditory signature most listeners hear as definingly Jewish.

name: Russian minor-key estrada / shanson harmonic vocabulary
sub: Russian sentimental popular-song minor-key vocabulary
note: The defining harmonic vocabulary of Russian sentimental popular song — minor-key default (Aeolian and Harmonic minor) with characteristic chromatic descent through the natural minor seventh, the half-step approach to the dominant from below, and the "Russian romance" (russkiy romans) chord progression of i - V/iv - iv - V - i. Traceable from the 19th-century salon romance tradition through the early-20th-century gypsy romance (tsyganskiy romans), the Soviet estrada commercial pop, the bardic / avtorskaya pesnya tradition, and the post-Soviet shanson genre.

name: Congolese rumba / soukous chanson-then-seben form
sub: Congolese rumba / soukous structural form with sebene guitar-improvisation finale
note: The defining structural-rhythmic framework of Congolese rumba and its faster-tempo derivation soukous — every song follows a two-part chanson-then-sebene structure: first half (chanson) is the slower-tempo sung verse-and-chorus song-form in moderate 4/4 (90-110 BPM) with the rumba feel inherited from Cuban son brought back to the Congo via the GV series 78 records in the 1940s-50s; second half (sebene, French-derived from "seven" referring to the 7th-chord harmonic vocabulary of the section) accelerates to faster tempo (130-180 BPM) where the band breaks into pure dance-floor groove with the lead guitar (mi-solo) and rhythm guitar (mi-composé) playing interlocking single-note melodic patterns over chordal-bass-and-percussion. The codified soukous mi-solo and mi-composé guitar interlock established by Dr. Nico (Nicolas Kasanda) and Franco (Luambo Makiadi) became the genres global signature.

name: Swahili taarab Eastern modal vocabulary
sub: East African Swahili-coast taarab maqam-derived modal vocabulary
note: The modal vocabulary of Swahili coastal East African taarab — a synthesis of Arab maqam (the genre name itself derives from the Arabic word for "to delight" or "to entertain", and the modal vocabulary is largely Arab-borrowed), Indian classical raga influence (from East African coastal Indian communities and the Bombay HMV recording infrastructure that produced the first commercial recordings of taarab in 1928), and Bantu-Swahili language poetry. Primary modes used: Bayati, Rast, Hijaz, Saba, Nahawand — the same makam-derived modes used in Egyptian, Levantine, and Greek rebetiko, but with distinct East African phrase-vocabulary and call-and-response chorus answering structures. Distinct from straight Arab tarab (which has solo-virtuoso vocal foreground) by its large ensemble and dance-functional character.

name: Mande pentatonic jeli modal vocabulary
sub: Mande griot pentatonic-and-heptatonic modal vocabulary
note: The modal vocabulary of Mande jeli (griot) traditional music spanning Mali, Guinea, Senegal, Gambia, Burkina Faso. Two principal modal systems coexist: pentatonic (used for older repertoire and the Sosso tradition, exemplified by the Sosso bala balafon in Niagassola, Guinea, the anchor of Mande musical heritage) and heptatonic (used for Maninka repertoire and the modern kora playing tradition, with the balafon tuned to seven-near-equal divisions of the octave, similar to Thai equal-heptatonic). The 21-string kora is tuned to two octaves of heptatonic scale in either silaba (with one of two characteristic mode-shifts) or tomora (the other shift). The jeli singer treats the harmonic-instrumental accompaniment as a backdrop against which to deliver epic recitation of genealogical-historical material (Sundiata Keita epic, Almami Samori epic, lineage-praise for specific patron families).

name: Yoruba juju / fuji polyrhythmic talking-drum vocabulary
sub: Yoruba Nigerian polyrhythmic talking-drum-led popular music vocabulary
note: The defining rhythmic-melodic framework of Yoruba Nigerian popular music — juju and fuji, the two principal Yoruba-language post-colonial popular music genres. Both build on the same Yoruba traditional foundation of dundun (talking drum) family, bata drum battery (Yoruba religious-derived percussion), and call-and-response praise-singing in Yoruba language. Juju (codified from 1960 onward) adds electric-guitar interlocking-pattern foreground, electric bass, modest drum kit. Fuji (codified from 1965 onward) keeps the percussion-only acoustic instrumentation but expands the dundun battery to 6-8 drummers.

name: Iraqi maqam jazil (Baghdadi maqam school)
sub: Iraqi maqam classical vocal modal system
note: The Iraqi maqam (al-Maqam al-Iraqi) modal system — distinct from the broader Arab maqam tradition by its specific Baghdadi corpus of 56 named maqams (mode-pieces, each with a specific opening tahrir vocal cadenza, a body section called miyana, and a closing teslim cadence), its vocal-foregrounded performance practice (the solo qari vocalist is the canonical figure, not the instrumentalists), its small chalghi ensemble (santur as dominant accompaniment, jawza Iraqi spike-fiddle, tabla, riq) rather than the larger oud-qanun-violin orchestras of Egyptian-Levantine tarab, and its repertoire of mufrad single-stanza or sequenced bestat-and-pestat poetic settings drawn from classical Arabic, post-classical colloquial Iraqi Arabic, Persian, and Turkish poetic corpora. The modal system uses the same microtonal Arabic quartertone intervals (24-step quartertone scale per octave) as the broader maqam world but with characteristically Iraqi mode-modulation patterns.

name: Moroccan Andalusī nūba eleven-mode cycle
sub: Moroccan / Maghrebi Andalusi classical 11-nūba cycle modal system
note: The Moroccan Andalusī nūba modal system — a cycle of 11 surviving nūba (multi-section suites, each in a single mode, lasting 4-7 hours when performed complete), each nūba named for its core mode. Each nūba moves through 5 progressive rhythmic-tempo sections (mizan): basit (free), qaim wa-nusf (6/4), btayhi (8/4), darj (4/4), quddam (3/4 or 6/8 accelerating). The 11-nūba cycle is the surviving fragment of an originally 24-nūba cycle. The Algerian gharnati and Tunisian malouf traditions are sister Maghrebi-Andalusi lineages.

name: Hindustani thaat-system raga performance form (alap-jod-jhala-gat)
sub: Hindustani classical raga performance form
note: The defining performance-form framework of Hindustani classical raga music — every solo instrumental or vocal performance of a raga moves through structured sections, each developing the raga progressively: alap (slow unmetered introduction exploring the raga modal interval-vocabulary and characteristic phrase-patterns, can last 20-45 minutes on a major concert performance), jod (medium-tempo pulse section, melodic phrases now anchored to a developing rhythmic pulse, no tabla yet), jhala (fast rhythmic-figure section, on plucked instruments characterized by the rapid sympathetic-string strumming pattern that gives the section its name), then the composed gat / bandish (composition) with tabla accompaniment that develops through bols (rhythmic syllable patterns), laykari (rhythmic variation), and tihai (three-fold cadence closures). The 10-thaat system organizes the universe of Hindustani ragas into 10 parent scale-types codified by V.N. Bhatkhande in the early 20th century (Bilawal, Khamaj, Kafi, Asavari, Bhairavi, Bhairav, Kalyan, Marwa, Purvi, Todi). Time-of-day association (each raga has a prescribed performance time of day or season) is a central organizing principle.

name: Carnatic 72-melakarta scale-system kriti performance form
sub: Carnatic classical raga 72-melakarta and kriti-composition form
note: The defining performance-form framework of Carnatic classical music — distinct from Hindustani classical in being composition-foregrounded rather than modal-improvisation-foregrounded. The Carnatic concert (kutcheri) is built around a sequence of pre-composed kritis (devotional songs) by the canonical early-19th-century composers and the broader Carnatic composer canon. Each kriti has the standard three-part structure: pallavi (refrain), anupallavi (second section that develops upward toward the upper octave), and charanam (longer extending section). The 72-melakarta system codified in 1620 organizes Carnatic ragas into 72 parent scales.

name: Jamaican riddim vocabulary (one-drop, steppers, rockers, rub-a-dub)
sub: Jamaican reggae rhythm-section vocabulary
note: The defining rhythm-section vocabulary of Jamaican reggae and its derivatives — built on four canonical drum patterns established in the 1970s. One-drop: the kick drum is silent on beat 1 and lands only on beat 3 alongside the snares cross-stick (the canonical roots reggae feel). Steppers: kick on every beat (1, 2, 3, 4), giving a driving four-on-the-floor reggae feel that emerged in the mid-1970s alongside roots reggaes apocalyptic-prophetic lyrical content. Rockers: kick on beats 1 and 3 with characteristic timbale fills (the Channel One studio sound of the late 70s). Rub-a-dub: slower mid-tempo dancehall pocket (80-95 BPM) that bridges roots reggae and early dancehall in the early 1980s. The bass guitar plays the riddim line as a foreground melodic-rhythmic voice, not just a harmonic foundation.

name: Trinidad calypso / soca 2/4 rhythmic vocabulary
sub: Trinidadian calypso and soca 2/4 dance-rhythm framework
note: The defining rhythmic framework of Trinidadian calypso and its faster-tempo dance derivation soca — the 2/4 meter (typically counted as a fast 4/4 in two-beat groupings) with characteristic syncopated tres-and-cuatro guitar pattern, iron section percussion (the "kaiso iron" played on brake-drum, ironside-of-a-truck, or steel hand-percussion), conga-and-bongo battery, and the kaiso call-and-response vocal structure (the chantwell singer calls, the crowd or backing chorus responds). Calypso operates at 110-130 BPM with elaborated narrative-and-topical content; soca (codified in 1973) operates at 140-170 BPM with simpler call-and-response party-anthem content. The post-1980s soca extension into Power Soca (extra-fast, 160+ BPM) and Groovy Soca (mid-tempo 100-120 BPM) gave the genre internal subgenre vocabulary.

name: Haitian kompa-direkt meringue rhythm
sub: Haitian kompa-direkt dance rhythm vocabulary
note: The defining rhythmic framework of Haitian kompa-direkt — invented in 1955 as a slower 2/4 derivation of the broader Caribbean meringue rhythmic foundation, distinct from the Dominican merengue (which is faster, 130-150 BPM) and from the kindred Haitian cadence-rampa lineage (a parallel innovation). Kompa operates at 90-110 BPM with characteristic tcha-tcha-tcha percussion-syncopation pattern, big-band horn-section arrangement, and lyrical content alternating French and Haitian Creole.

name: Hard rock / metal blues-pentatonic-and-power-chords vocabulary
sub: Distorted-electric hard rock and metal harmonic vocabulary
note: The defining harmonic-textural framework of hard rock, metal, and their subgenres — built on the blues pentatonic minor scale (1-flat3-4-5-flat7) as the soloing default vocabulary, power chords (root-fifth-octave, no third) as the rhythm-section harmonic foundation (making major-or-minor tonality ambiguous), heavily distorted electric guitar as the timbral foreground, and drop tunings (drop D for most NWOBHM and grunge, drop C and lower for stoner / doom / sludge / modern metalcore) as the standard re-tuning practice. The palm-muting chugged-riff technique creates the characteristic percussive-rhythmic foundation of thrash and modern metal. Twin-guitar harmony (harmonized leads in thirds or sixths) became the canonical melodic-lead technique of NWOBHM and Gothenburg melodic death metal. Distinct from blues rock (which retains blues idiom intact, less distortion, less metal-vocabulary) and from progressive rock (which uses more complex harmonic vocabulary including jazz extensions).

name: Doom metal tritone / diminished vocabulary
sub: Doom metal slow-tempo tritone-and-diminished modal vocabulary
note: The defining harmonic-modal framework of doom metal and its derivatives (traditional doom, stoner metal, sludge metal, post-metal) — built on the slow-tempo (50-80 BPM) foregrounding of the tritone interval (augmented fourth / diminished fifth, the "diabolus in musica" of medieval music theory) and characteristic Locrian modal vocabulary that the tritone implies. The early-70s British template (the canonical 1970 doom recording opens with the iconic tritone B-F riff in F) established the genre vocabulary. Subsequent doom subgenres developed the template in different directions: traditional doom retains the slow tempo and the original chord vocabulary; stoner metal adds blues-rock vocabulary and lower-tuned guitars; sludge metal adds hardcore-punk vocal aggression; post-metal adds long-form instrumental composition and ambient textural sections.

name: Shoegaze / dream pop chromatic-modal vocabulary
sub: Shoegaze and dream pop harmonic-textural vocabulary
note: The defining harmonic-textural framework of shoegaze and dream pop — built on chromatic non-diatonic chord movement, heavy use of tremolo-and-glide detuning (the early-90s glide-guitar technique), reverb and delay as foundational textural processing rather than mix accent, dense overlapping multi-guitar layers, and buried-in-mix female-or-androgynous vocals that function as another textural layer rather than narrative-foregrounded melody.

name: Country Nashville three-chord train-beat vocabulary
sub: Nashville country I-IV-V three-chord and train-beat rhythmic framework
note: The defining harmonic-rhythmic framework of mid-20th-century commercial country music — built on the I-IV-V three-chord progression as the harmonic foundation (often with added vi minor for the bridge or chorus pivot), the train beat (2/4 shuffle with eighth-note ride-cymbal driving rhythm, derived from train-wheel-clacking onomatopoeia) as the canonical Nashville rhythm-section pattern, and the Nashville Number System (the chord-chart shorthand that uses numbers instead of letter names to communicate progressions between session musicians, codified in the 1950s). The lead instrumentation centers on pedal steel guitar (E9 tuning for the standard Nashville crying-steel sound, C6 tuning for the western-swing jazz-influenced sound), Telecaster electric guitar with chicken-pickin technique, fiddle, and acoustic guitar rhythm-foundation. Subgenres specialize the framework: honky-tonk (faster shuffle, harder edges), bakersfield (the West Coast extension of honky-tonk), Nashville Sound (smoother pop crossover with strings-and-chorus production), outlaw country (the 1970s back-to-roots reaction against Nashville Sound).

name: Bluegrass high-lonesome pentatonic vocabulary
sub: Bluegrass high-tenor vocal and pentatonic-modal vocabulary
note: The defining vocal-and-instrumental vocabulary of bluegrass — built on the high-lonesome vocal tradition (the canonical high-tenor lead-vocal style, often in close harmony with a baritone and bass), pentatonic and Mixolydian-mode melodic vocabulary descended from Anglo-Celtic ballad and Appalachian old-time fiddle traditions, three-finger banjo roll (the canonical style from 1945 onward, the right-hand pattern that revolutionized banjo playing), mandolin canonical style (the chop-and-tremolo right-hand technique that turns the mandolin into a rhythmic-and-melodic foundation instrument), fiddle in standard tuning or cross-tuning (the AEAE or AEAC# tunings that give old-time and bluegrass fiddle their characteristic drone-and-double-stop sound), and the breakdown fast-tempo (often 180-220 BPM) instrumental-virtuoso showcase form.

name: Rockabilly 1950s walking-bass slap rhythm
sub: 1950s rockabilly slap-bass and electric-guitar vocabulary
note: The defining rhythmic-and-instrumental framework of 1950s rockabilly — built on the slap-bass technique (upright string bass played with percussive thumb-slap), electric guitar (Gretsch hollowbody with Bigsby tremolo, Fender Telecaster, played with travis-picking right-hand technique and the canonical Sun Studios slapback short-tape-delay processing), drums (sometimes minimal), and lead vocal in the style codified at Sun Studios Memphis under Sam Phillips production. The harmonic vocabulary fuses country I-IV-V three-chord foundation with blues pentatonic vocabulary.

name: Iberian kantautor minority-language modal vocabulary
sub: Iberian Peninsula minority-language singer-songwriter harmonic-and-modal vocabulary
note: The defining harmonic-and-modal framework of Iberian Peninsula minority-language kantautor traditions — Basque (Euskera), Galician (Galego), Catalan, with parallel Aranés Occitan and Asturian minor traditions. Characterized by acoustic-guitar fingerpicked or strummed accompaniment in open or DADGAD-adjacent tunings, modal melodic vocabulary drawing on regional traditional song-corpora (the Galician Cantigas de Santa María corpus from the 13th-century Alfonso X court, the Basque trikitixa diatonic-accordion folk substrate, the Catalan sardana circle-dance modal vocabulary), and lyrical content explicitly engaged with minority-language cultural-political revival in the post-Franco democratic period (1975-onward). Distinct from Spanish-language Castilian cantautor (which has its own canon centered on Joaquín Sabina, Luis Eduardo Aute, Joan Manuel Serrats Spanish-language work) by its minority-language vehicular and explicit cultural-political reclamation focus.

name: Sephardi / Hasidic / Cantorial Jewish modal vocabulary
sub: Jewish liturgical and paraliturgical modal system across Sephardi and Ashkenazi traditions
note: The Jewish liturgical and paraliturgical modal vocabulary spanning the Sephardi and Ashkenazi traditions — distinct but parallel mode-systems serving the same liturgical functions across two distinct musical lineages. Sephardi modal vocabulary: Arab maqam-derived modes (Maqam Rast, Bayati, Hijaz, Saba, Nahawand, Ajam, Sikah) adapted for liturgical-Hebrew and paraliturgical-Ladino content, with the canonical Aleppo / Salonica / Tetouan bakkashot tradition pairing specific maqam with specific liturgical-poetic content. Ashkenazi modal vocabulary: the shtayger (mode) system of Eastern European synagogue chant, with principal modes Ahava Raba (Freygish, Phrygian dominant), Mi Sheberach (Ukrainian Dorian), Magen Avot (natural minor), Adonai Malach (Mixolydian-derived) — the same modal corpus shared with secular klezmer. Hasidic niggun tradition adapts these modes to wordless melody (niggun, plural niggunim) in dynastic-court-specific repertoire (Modzitz dynasty noted for its musical creativity).

name: Mediterranean traditional polyphonic-modal vocabulary
sub: Mediterranean traditional vocal polyphony and modal melodic vocabulary
note: The defining modal-and-polyphonic vocabulary of traditional Mediterranean and adjacent multi-voice vocal traditions — Sardinian cantu a tenore four-voice male polyphony, Corsican paghjella male trio polyphony, Albanian iso-polyphony, Bulgarian Shopluk female polyphony, Georgian three-voice polyphony, and the broader Mediterranean parallel-and-overlapping polyphonic vocal heritage that preserves pre-tempered intervals within pastoral-village vocal practice.

name: Andean Colombian bambuco / pasillo 6/8 vocabulary
sub: Colombian Andean string-trio rhythmic and harmonic framework
note: The defining rhythmic-harmonic framework of Andean Colombian string-trio music — bambuco (the canonical 6/8 Colombian national rhythm, with characteristic three-against-two syncopation between tiple strumming foundation and melodic line; the tiple bass-note hits on beats 1 and 4 of the 6/8 measure while the syncopated upper-voice strumming pattern creates the genres distinctive bambuco-pegado feel), pasillo (the Colombian-and-Ecuadorian fast-waltz derivation of the European-derived 19th-century pasillo dance, often instrumental virtuoso showcases), torbellino (the Boyacá-Cundinamarca folk-dance rhythm in fast 3/4), guabina (the Santander-Boyacá pastoral 6/8 song-form). The harmonic vocabulary uses I-IV-V three-chord foundation common to many Andean and pan-Latin-American traditions, with frequent modulation to relative minor for the bridge section. The tiple-and-bandola-andina-and-guitar trio is the canonical instrumental configuration, the bandola playing rapid melodic single-note runs over the tiple chordal foundation.

name: Pan-Latin bolero 2/4 romantic ballad vocabulary
sub: Pan-Latin-American bolero romantic-ballad harmonic and rhythmic vocabulary
note: The defining harmonic-rhythmic framework of pan-Latin-American bolero — slow 2/4 meter (typically 60-80 BPM), characteristic bolero rhythm of long-short-long-short cinquillo, harmonic vocabulary built on major-minor modulation, and instrumentation centered on the bolero trio (two guitars plus requinto plus close-harmony vocal trio).

name: Tin Pan Alley 32-bar AABA song form vocabulary
sub: Pre-rock American popular song 32-bar AABA form and harmonic vocabulary
note: The defining song-form framework of pre-rock American popular songwriting (c. 1915-1965) — the 32-bar AABA form (two 8-bar A sections stating the main theme, an 8-bar B section bridge providing harmonic and melodic contrast, then the final 8-bar A return) became the canonical Broadway-show-tune and Tin-Pan-Alley pop song structure. Earlier songs often used verse-chorus structure where the verse (8-16 bars of recitative-narrative setup) preceded the canonical 32-bar AABA chorus (the part that became standalone in jazz instrumental performance). The harmonic vocabulary draws on the extended jazz harmonic palette: ii-V-I cadences, secondary dominants, tritone substitutions, diminished passing chords, modal interchange between parallel major and minor. The songwriter craft is built on the Brill Building infrastructure: lyricist-composer partnerships (Rodgers and Hart, Lerner and Loewe, Goffin and King, Bacharach and David) developing songs to fit specific commissioned performers, with publisher-as-intermediary distributing songs across performers, films, and Broadway productions.

name: Hip-hop breakbeat sample-collage boom-bap vocabulary
sub: NYC hip-hop breakbeat-and-sampler-collage rhythmic and textural vocabulary
note: The defining rhythmic-and-textural framework of canonical NYC hip-hop from the pre-sampling era through the golden-age boom-bap era — built on the breakbeat foundation, the SP-1200 and Akai S950 sampler era of 1986-1991, turntablism, and the four-bar-loop extended-structure song form.

name: West / North African mbalax / rai polyrhythmic vocabulary
sub: Senegalese mbalax and Algerian rai harmonic and rhythmic vocabulary
note: The defining harmonic-rhythmic vocabulary of West African mbalax (Senegalese) and North African rai (Algerian) — two parallel late-1970s African popular-music genres that emerged from regional folk-substrate-and-modern-band-instrumentation fusion. Mbalax: built on the polyrhythmic Senegalese sabar drum-battery foundation (the sabar is a Wolof family of single-headed drums with characteristic asymmetric rhythmic patterns) extended with electric guitar, electric bass, and synth keyboard, plus Wolof-language lead vocal. Rai: built on the Oran Algerian raï-traditional-vocal foundation (originally bedouin praise-poetry) extended with synthesizers, drum machines, electric guitar, and saxophone, with Algerian Arabic-language vocal foreground. Both genres share characteristic pentatonic-and-modal melodic vocabulary derived from their respective regional folk substrates and rhythmic-syncopation-foreground production aesthetics.

name: Southeast Asian pentatonic popular-vocal vocabulary
sub: Indonesian dangdut / Thai-Lao mor lam / Vietnamese chamber pentatonic vocal vocabulary
note: The defining pentatonic-and-modal vocabulary of Southeast Asian popular-and-traditional vocal genres — covering Indonesian dangdut (the working-class popular genre that emerged in late-1960s Jakarta fusing Indian filmi rhythms, Malay popular song, and rock elements, codified from 1973 onward, with pentatonic modal vocabulary derived from Malay folk substrate), Thai-Lao mor lam (the Isaan / Lao popular vocal-and-khaen-bamboo-mouth-organ tradition with characteristic Lao pentatonic modal vocabulary), Vietnamese nhạc tài tử (southern amateur chamber tradition) and ca trù (central Vietnamese sung-poetry tradition with pentatonic modal vocabulary distinct from Chinese pentatonic systems), and the Bangkok Theravada Buddhist temple Pali-language scriptural-recitation tradition (modal melismatic chant of the Tipitaka scripture-canon). Distinct from East Asian pentatonic systems (Chinese, Japanese, Korean) by its specific Southeast Asian regional modal-vocabulary inflections.

name: Istrian scale (Croatian non-tempered six-tone)
sub: paired-second intervals; cadential endings strictly unison or octave
note: Croatian Istrian non-tempered six-tone scale codified in the 1920s by Ivan Matetić Ronjgov. Characteristic paired-second intervals. Cadential endings strictly in unison or octave. Used in Istrian dvoglasje two-part diaphonic singing and sopele paired-double-reed-shawm playing. Region: Istria peninsula, Croatia.

name: Lithuanian sutartinės parallel-seconds vocabulary
sub: narrow range; parallel major-second intervals between voices
note: Lithuanian sutartinės parallel-seconds vocabulary. Narrow range (two-to-five pitches). Characteristic parallel major-second intervals between voices. Strict canonical imitation at the second or fourth. Considered one of the most archaic tonal systems in Europe.

name: Coptic Orthodox microtonal modal system
sub: diatonic base with characteristic shifted thirds
note: Coptic Orthodox liturgical microtonal modal system. Diatonic base with characteristic shifted thirds. Mode-specific cadential formulae. Documented by Ragheb Moftah, Ernest Newlandsmith, and Margit Tóth in twentieth-century transcription projects.

name: Mongolian pentatonic long-song modal vocabulary
sub: pentatonic base with melismatic ornament and falsetto-chest alternation
note: Mongolian pentatonic modal vocabulary characteristic of urtiin duu long-song. Pentatonic mode base. Wide melodic range with melismatic ornament extending single syllables across many beats. Characteristic falsetto-chest-register alternation. Also used in khoomei and Tuvan kargyraa-sygyt contexts.

name: Ethiopian qenet pentatonic mode-system
sub: five pentatonic modes with pure-temperament intonation
note: Ethiopian qenet pentatonic mode-system (unified reference for tradition-level mode selection). Five canonical modes: tizita (nostalgic), bati (praise), ambassel (festive), anchihoye (mournful), and minor-mode tezeta variants. Pure-temperament, not equal-tempered. Used in azmari, pop, and secular repertoires.

name: Sámi narrow-range pentatonic-leaning yoik vocabulary
sub: two-to-five pitches; pre-tempered Arctic Finno-Ugric system
note: Sámi narrow-range melodic vocabulary characteristic of yoik (luohti, leuʹdd, vuelie variants). Two-to-five pitches; pentatonic-leaning; characteristic fourth, fifth, and octave intervals. Pre-tempered system. Distinguished from related Karelian rune-singing by absence of strict alternation between text-bearing and answer voices.

name: Performer-relative intonation
sub: intonation by ear; no interval ratios asserted
note: A recording-model option for oral practices when the cited source does not specify a measured pitch system. It asserts neither equal temperament nor just-intonation ratios; local melodic organization remains performer-dependent.

name: Unpitched percussion
sub: rhythmic sound without an assigned scale
note: Use for percussion-only ensembles without a documented pitch scale. Relative drum register is controlled on each instrument, not represented as a Western temperament.
